subtopic: DEPORTATION OF TWO REFUGEES FROM YUGOSLAVIA

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. E, D. Fulton (Kamloops): I should like to ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration if he is in a position to give the house some information with regard to the position and the fate of two persons who have been referred to in the press as refugees from Yugoslavia. I am not able to pronounce their names, but I told the minister that I should like to ask the question and I think he knows the cases to which I refer. Can he say whether it is established whether or not these men are genuine political refugees?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DEPORTATION OF TWO REFUGEES FROM YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
The two gentlemen concerned are at present in detention quarters in Montreal. They are citizens of Yugoslavia. One is a married man of about 33 years of age; the other is a young man of about 22. The latter has a passport from the Yugoslavian government which, so far as we know, is valid. The former has no papers of any kind. They both left Yugoslavia last July, proceeded through Austria and Germany to a port on the North sea, stowed away on board ship and eventually were picked up in Toronto.
They were ordered deported as stowaways because that is our policy. We do not accept people who do not conform to our immigration regulations. In the course of examination they both said they had been informed in the refugee camp where they had spent a short time in Germany that there was an easy means of getting to Canada if you stowed away at a particular port on board ship. Consequently we are doing our best to prevent this from being a fact, and in particular we are deporting these people so that it may be learned that we do not accept immigrants in this way.
However, I know there are certain people who felt that ir: these two cases these persons might possibly suffer because of their actions
(Mr. MacLean.l
should they be returned to their native country. I point out again that the one has a valid passport, so far as we know. I point out also that any deportation order we may issue would only mean that they would be taken in custody by the shipping line whence they came to Canada, and would in the normal course go back to the port in Germany from which they came. We do not make a practice of deporting people behind the iron curtain unless there are most unusual circumstances.

My hon. friend will appreciate the fact that the wheat board takes delivery of wheat at three principal marketing places, namely Fort William-Port Arthur, Vancouver and Churchill. To market the wheat from Fort William in the winter season it must be shipped by rail to Halifax or Saint John and transportation charges have to be added to the Fort William price, which puts sales from those ports somewhat out of line with those from Vancouver.

It has been a rule of the department for several years that we do not discuss the marketing of wheat from the current crop. I think my hon. friend will appreciate the necessity for that. The wheat board is dealing with customers around the world, and anything I say here is reflected as being the views of the wheat board. Comments from me are not helpful to its operations.
Representations are being made to the government of the United States almost every week, just as representations are being made to us by the United States. I know of no plan for a fire sale in the United States. That country has a certain program that has dangers to Canada inherent in it if recklessly used, a program of giving assistance to foreign countries in the form of foodstuffs. We have reason to believe that it will be used with due regard to friendly countries who also have marketing problems. But, as I say, the situation is being watched carefully. Our people are in Washington and people from Washington are here frequently to discuss that particular problem, and we have every reason to believe that the United States will co-operate with Canada in order to see that the Canadian position is not damaged.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR INQUIRY INTO INCREASED PRICE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REQUEST FOR INQUIRY INTO INCREASED PRICE
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice arising out of a report in this morning's press that there will be an immediate and substantial increase in the price of coffee. Will the Minister of Justice direct that an inquiry be made into this matter, as President Eisenhower has directed in the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REQUEST FOR INQUIRY INTO INCREASED PRICE
speechtext:
I wish to thank my hon. friend for sending me notice of his question which, unfortunately, reached me only a moment or two before the house opened. However, I may say that the report which appeared in this morning's Montreal Gazette, and which is perhaps the one to which my hon. friend is referring, indicates pretty clearly on its face one of the main reasons for the increase in the price of coffee. Due to frost damage in the coffee plantations of Brazil the normal production of some 16 million bags of coffee in that country has been cut down to 14 million bags and, what is probably more serious, the frost damage to Brazil's young trees is so extensive that it appears that Brazilian production for the next several years may be severely limited, in this way reducing the world supply.
On the face of this news item, therefore, it would appear that the rise in the price of coffee is perhaps attributable to these natural causes. In the combines investigation branch we are interested in rises in the prices of things which are attributable to other than natural causes, in other words to combines and to attempts to rig prices. It is true that we watch the prices of these commodities carefully to make sure that a price rise which is under observation is not attributable to a combine, and for that reason we take an interest in such matters as the present price of coffee.
But our inquiries would seem to support another item which appears in this morning's Montreal Gazette, wherein it is stated that while Toronto importers predicted that the price of coffee would increase by about 34 cents a pound to $1.33 in the next few months, Ottawa importers did not believe the price would go that high and predicted a rise of two or three cents. Our price checks have indicated that the price rise here has been more of the order of that mentioned by the Ottawa importers.
My hon. friend asks whether we will authorize an inquiry along the lines of that authorized by President Eisenhower in the United States. According to press reports President Eisenhower instructed the federal trade commission of the United States of America to make a full-scale investigation. I would say that we would not authorize a full-scale investigation here unless it appeared, from the checks we are now making, that it was necessary. In that connection, having regard to the fact that the United States is by far the largest purchaser of coffee in the world, the price which it pays for its coffee tends to fix the price of the

coffee that is bought in Canada, so the investigation by the United States, if it discloses anything at all, would probably disclose the causes or some of the causes for the increase that is taking place or will take place here. '

The other day the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough) asked a question with respect to the new vaccine, and I should now like to give further information.
Research on poliomyelitis vaccine has been carried on at the Connaught laboratories during the past two or three years, and has contributed greatly to the production of the large supplies to be used in the extensive testing of this vaccine in the United States. The value of the vaccine has not yet been established and may not be established for some time. Consideration was given by the officials of my department and by the dominion council of health to the institution of similar testing in Canada. But on the basis of the information we have and of the advice we have received from experts in this field, the department has concluded that the proper course for us for the time being is to observe the very extensive trial already launched in the United States, with the knowledge that the information resulting from the trial will be completely at our disposal and may be used as a guide in determining the need for and the nature of further action in this country.
As outlined in the reply which my parliamentary assistant gave to the house on December 2 last, the government has already undertaken to provide substantial assistance toward measures to combat poliomyelitis in Canada. I wish again to assure the house that we are prepared to play our full part in ensuring that the people of this country will enjoy the benefits of any outstanding advances in the prevention of this dread disease.

I want to say that we are happy to have the money, and by the end of June we will have many more houses ready for old age pensioners on a low rental basis.
I am not quite certain whether I understood the minister when he answered a question just a few moments ago concerning loans that had been made, I believe, in Quebec.

speechtext: In Ottawa.

subsubtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Did I understand the minister to say that, in part, the loan concerned old age pensioners, for whom houses would be built on an average rental basis of $58 per month? There we have a clear indication of the need for federal action, either by direct aid or by lowering the interest rate, because I do not know of any old age pensioners or low income groups who could pay $58 per month. We do know, because it has been proven over a period of years, that if the provincial government has an interest, and the federal government gives an interest rate through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation equal to the government's long term rate, you can supply fully modern houses to people in the low income groups for $20 or $21 per month, on a self-supporting basis. That is being done in British Columbia, and being done I point out even with the high rate which does not enable you to do as much building as you would otherwise, or give the rental that you otherwise could.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, to give the house the benefit of our accountant's report on the first five loans that we secured from the government. On project No. 1 we borrowed $10,000, amortized over 20 years, and the

interest rate was 3 per cent. By the time we pay it back it will have cost us in all $13,443. On the second project we borrowed $25,000 amortized over 40 years at 3 per cent, and that is going to cost us $43,262.40. On project No. 3 we borrowed $20,000 amortized over 40 years at 3 per cent, and that will cost us $34,610 by the time it is repaid. On project No. 4 we stepped it up and borrowed $60,000 amortized over 40 years, and the government established a rate of 3-5 per cent. We shall have paid back $111,940.80 by the time the loan has been paid. On project No. 5 we borrowed $55,000 and the interest rate was up to 3J per cent, amortized over 40 years. This loan will cost us $106,624. In other words, borrowing through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for old age pensioners on a non-profit basis, with a provincial grant of one-third and getting the land for one dollar from the municipality, we have borrowed $170,000 and will have to pay back $309,880.20. When we have to pay back that amount of money for this amount we borrowed, under the best terms the government gives, what then is the position of the citizen who wants to build his own home and has to borrow at 5-5 or 6 per cent?
I believe it can be said without question that not only is the down payment difficult but housing costs are high. I sincerely hope the minister will tell us some time just what use has been made over a period of years of that section of the housing act which gives him almost unlimited powers of research to try to bring down housing costs in Canada. All these factors, the heavy down payment, the high cost of housing, the interest rate and so on, hold back many people from building their own homes or building low rental homes.
I feel very strongly that, in view of the urgent need for houses in Canada both for home ownership and for rental, the government would be taking a very commendable and advisable step if it would do one of two things, either directly subsidize housing by a reduction of the interest rate to 2 per cent or grant a subsidy. This would provide a stopgap for the serious unemployment situation.
If the government does not feel it is possible to reduce the interest rate, then in the interests of housing, and of employment, they should extend to those who desire to construct houses in Canada the same provisions that have been established for years in connection with other types of houses constructed by limited liability companies or nonprofit organizations. This would enable people to obtain money at the long term interest rate of the federal government. It would
National Housing Act
mean at least a reduction of 14 or 2 per cent in the interest rate; and when you are borrowing for 25, 30 or 35 years the saving would amount to a great deal and would be an encouragement to housing construction in Canada.
So, Mr. Speaker, I sincerely hope that the minister, having established a good principle some years ago on one type of construction, will carry forward that same principle in the greater field of home construction in Canada, and either make grants directly in aid of home construction or reduce the interest rate to not more than the long term borrowing rate of the government.
I suggest this would be welcomed by every member in the house and by the people of Canada generally, and would amply demonstrate that we do have a progressive government and a progressive parliament.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Order. I believe the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) wishes to proceed.

subsubtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the first place I should like to congratulate the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) and the government for introducing this new housing legislation which I believe is sound, progressive, and tailored to meet the needs of the Canadian people.
The two provisions which I feel will be of particular assistance in helping more people to acquire homes will be the lower down payment and the longer amortization period in which to pay back the mortgage. This means that people will have to pay less when the house is purchased, and will pay less in the monthly carrying charges.
I would also commend the government on making available loans from banks. I note this has been done in most, if not all, western countries, and it would seem to be the logical development of the Canadian banking system. Unlike my hon. friend the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), I am not a bit worried about the novelty of the idea. It seems to have worked successfully in other countries, and undoubtedly the elasticity and ingenuity of our banking system here will permit of its being of great assistance in the further development of the Canadian economy.
I am particularly intrigued by the fact that these insured mortgages can be used as collateral to be deposited with the central bank by the chartered bank, which in return will receive credit the same as for Canadian

National Housing Act
bonds. This is indeed far-reaching, and I believe takes into consideration in a brilliant manner the need for credit expansion in an ever-growing economy.
There is one thing, however, that does disturb me at the present time in this country, and that is the fact that the little man, the clerk or the factory worker, whose annual income is less than $3,000, cannot buy a home under the National Housing Act because the carrying charges comprise more than 23 per cent of his gross income. It seems to me fundamental justice that such a man should be able to own a house as well as anyone else. Accordingly, I have gone to some trouble to ascertain what 'other countries have done, having particular regard for this problem.
I find that in no countries have houses been built for potential owners in the lower income brackets, and it would seem that the reason for this is that the risk of carrying a mortgage on a person with a marginal income is too great. A resultant foreclosure would not only take away a person's house but would result in the loss of his hard-earned down payment. Of course some of my friends, particularly in the C.C.F., will say, "Why not give an outright government subsidy to this man?" One answer would appear to be that in many cases an owner's income might improve to the point that the owner would not need the government subsidy; and then, of course, someone would be helped who would not need the help of the government.
I think, therefore, that subsidized government rental housing is the answer to the particular problem I have in mind, and I say that the new bill covers this in clause 36, formerly section 35 of the act. There is provision for joint development of lower cost rental housing between the provincial and federal governments. This is not pure theory; it has worked in practice. My information is that 1,562 units have been built so far under this clause, which was section 35 of the old act. The breakdown is as follows: 292 units in St. John's, Newfoundland; 161 units in Halifax; 288 units in Saint John, New Brunswick; 105 units in Saskatchewan; 224 units under construction in Vancouver, and 492 units in Ontario.
This scheme may be carried out in two ways-either by the owners buying the houses, which will cost less because no profit is being made by the developer of the lands from the installation of package disposal plants and the like, or by the appropriate government body renting the

houses, which is what I am more particularly concerned with here. The dwellings may be either duplexes or row houses, such as they have in Newfoundland, or single family dwelling houses, which have been confined largely to Ontario.
The important point is this, that the dwellings in Newfoundland rent at $37 or $38 per month, and at rentals of $55 to $60 a month on a self-liquidating basis. That seems to me to be the concrete answer to this problem of providing housing for the lower income groups. However, and this is the important thing, the initiative must come from the provinces under the legislation, or more specifically those creatures of the provinces, the local municipalities.
It is all very well for people to say, "Well, why do not the municipalities do something about it?" Those members in the house who have served on municipal councils in the last few years will realize that the problems of municipal councils are tremendous, and that the greatest problem of all is to provide funds for financing local schools. Let us be frank about it. This is a provincial matter. And I might say I am pained and disturbed that my esteemed friend, the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), got to his feet and complained that the bill does nothing about providing serviced land. I am sure he said that with his tongue in his cheek. Because my hon. friend knows-

I shall be glad to withdraw. I was saying that the providing of serviced land must come on the initiative of the provinces, and I would respectfully suggest to the hon. member for Eglinton that he use his considerable influence with his provincial colleagues in Ontario to see that installation of services goes forward in the Toronto area.
Just last week several large subdivisions were rejected by the planning board of the township of North York because of the lack of services. Is the hon. member for Eglinton seriously suggesting that this bill before the house should provide services for subdivisions? Hundreds of houses cannot be built in North York at the present time, and hundreds of families cannot have homes because the provincial government in Ontario has not seen fit to galvanize into action the metropolitan council of greater Toronto to provide serviced lands. The hon. member for Eglinton knows that. Therefore I respectfully ask, why does he draw a red herring across this trail? Why does he not come out and admit that this is a sound, imaginative bill? Why does he not admit that the problem of serviced land-the No. 1 problem in our housing bottleneck-is the ultimate and direct responsibility of the provincial government?
Again in closing, Mr. Speaker, I will say that I hope the provinces, the municipalities, and the federal government will all work together vigorously under the provisions of section 36 and solve our problem regarding low-cost rental housing. I think the explanation I have cited proves it can be done, and I fervently hope that more action will be taken in the near future.

subsubtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill reminds me of a measure to produce babies and leave them on the street. True, it does have clauses in it which can produce the swaddling clothes and the baskets to house babies temporarily, but it does not do what I think is necessary, namely look after the growth and the life of the structures it proposes to bring into being.
National Housing Act
I feel, and my over-all criticism of the bill is, that it does not provide sufficient precaution to see that the initial expenditure, the initial investment in the structure, is adequately protected, and I propose to enlarge on that. Today, with the extremely high cost of living, it is not so much the initial cost of a house that is causing the trouble for so many people; it is the problem of maintenance and upkeep of the house. The No. 1 problem, as I see it, is to relieve the burden, including the tax burden, which falls directly on the home owner.
The first protection which I consider the bill fails to give is a mandatory clause dealing with town planning. True, in the section dealing with housing redevelopment there is a clause making the municipality submit a proper plan for the redevelopment of blighted or slum areas. But the regulations in the section dealing with new construction and new development with regard to town planning are of a permissive nature. In my opinion, permissive is not enough. I have seen all too many housing developments start off with inadequate zoning or planning and become not actually blighted areas but areas where properties have decreased in value at a rate far more rapidly than in an area which was properly planned.
Therefore my first criticism of the bill would be that provision for town planning and zoning for all new construction should be made more mandatory, and at least require it to have the approval of the provincial authorities or the municipal board in the province of Ontario, and through them the architects of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or the town planners that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are using. That is the first point.
In that regard I think the remarks of the President of the United States are of some interest, because in dealing with this whole question of housing on January 26 he said that one of his provisions was this:
First, prevention of the spread of blight into good areas of the community through strict enforcement of housing and neighbourhood standards and strict occupancy controls.
Those of us who have seen the work that has been going on in the United States in regard to new development in the major cities can appreciate the importance being put on this question of proper planning. Therefore I feel that no new housing development should be started until, through planning, the future of the investment, no matter who makes it, will be as secure as possible and

National Housing Act that blight accelerated deterioration and the other dangerous developments which destroy the value of property will not set in.
It is all very well to have a beautiful, individually planned community; but if at some time in that planned community you are leaving it possible for somebody to come in and build a glue factory right next door, the whole value of that community will go down. In my opinion no new community should be created unless that protection is provided.
So much for town planning. The next criticism I have of the legislation-and I do not think this is so much the fault of the bill but rather the fault of the combines act-[DOT] is this. If the banks, who are not knowledgeable with regard to mortgages on real estate, which is an entirely new field to them, set up a company or some kind of organization in which all the banks could pool what resources they wished, and developed their own mortgage authority, it would probably be a good thing and certainly, I believe, would make for efficiency. But I doubt very much whether they would be able to do this because of the combines act, for I believe that banks getting together to form a company or trust to provide money for housing would probably contravene that act.
However, I would ask the minister to consult, if he will, with the law officers of the crown to see if that would be so, because there will be a lot of mortgage money not available if individual banks feel that in certain cases they have to provide for the servicing of mortgages in small communities, whereas if there was an association through which all the banks could co-operate I think it would be greatly to the advantage of the scheme. The United States system called the federal national mortgage association, or "Fanny Mae" to use the colloquial term, is a joint association and I do not know enough about it, but I feel it is providing a very desirable service in the United States.
Now I come directly to the cost of upkeep. Where the housing need is greatest is in the urban and particularly suburban or growth municipalities. My own is a case in point. In Toronto township, where I live, and in the part of Etobicoke township which I represent -two of the most rapidly growing townships in all of Canada-I would say that this year the assessments on property have multiplied between five and ten times. Some people will claim that while the assessments have gone up the mill rate also will go down drastically, and that is the devout hope of the Toronto metropolitan council. While the mill rate will go down, nevertheless the assessments have


gone up to such a degree that the net annual tax liability to the municipality by the home owner has in almost every case increased very substantially in the last three or four years. In most cases it has more than doubled since the end of the war, and in some cases it has not only doubled but trebled and quadrupled.
Municipal tax borne by the home owner is similar to a mortgage. You pay it or lose your property. Irrespective of your income, irrespective of your status or anything else, it is a direct liability on your prime security, that is your own home; yet the federal authorities, despite the fact that in the last budget they recognized the evils of double taxation and gave generous relief to the holders of Canadian common stocks and Canadian equities, are as yet blind to what I consider to be the most evil form of double taxation, namely taxation on the home of the Canadian citizen which must be paid but which is not considered when the individual home owner makes out his income tax form.
I have mentioned this before in this house, but I mention it again because I think it is only just that the municipal tax paid on a man's home should be a deduction from his income for the purpose of computing his income tax liability. But you will ask, "What about the man who rents? He has not that opportunity." But he has, because the landlord deducts municipal taxation and also the carrying charges, and in addition to that he amortizes over as many years as he likes the capital cost of the structure. The landlord, therefore, is by and large in a better position than the man who buys and owns. I feel that if we are going to encourage the man who buys and owns, then something along these lines must be done.
I am not going to go into the figures in detail in my own municipality, but I do want to say that the situation is definitely serious. If you undertake to construct a home on the basis of your income less the liabilities you have already undertaken, and if you have a tax liability which is constantly increasing, then your security is continually being whittled away by the continually rising costs of municipal government. I suggest that under these circumstances the first relief to the home owner should be in the matter of municipal taxation. I leave that for the moment, however, because I presume that will be one of the questions dealt with in the committee. Incidentally, I understand that municipal taxation is allowed as an income tax deduction in the United States.
My second point on the question of making it easier for a man to keep his home-and this is a problem I want to deal with-is that

I can see so easily the same conditions arising as in the thirties when a man bought a home, it deteriorated, and somebody along his street had a forced sale and sold at 50 or 60 cents on the dollar. What does that mean? It decreases the price of every single house on that street, because the forced sale regulates the price. I do not want people to be put in that position; therefore I am concentrating on making it easier to maintain the home.
Another way in which this bill is deficient is with regard to mortgage interest; not capital, but interest. In order to bring the man who owns his home into a position of equality with the man who rents, I believe that mortgage interest on a man's own home should also be allowed as a deduction from income for tax computation purposes.
Again the same thing holds true with regard to a man who builds a house and rents it. He can deduct the carrying charges. He can even amortize the capital cost, as he does. Then after the capital cost is amortized, he can sell the house	and	somebody else	willbe able to amortize	the	capital cost	on	thesame house. That is	the	situation if	he	hasbought for rental. I	do	not believe	that is
fair. I think encouragement must be given through the easing of the payments to keep the home. We have heard a great deal about insurance companies, banks, mortgage companies and everybody else asking so much in the way of interest and all the rest of it. The worst sinner or all is the federal government. It takes more from the income of the home owner than do all the other institutions combined. I feel that is the first place where relief should start.
The next point, of course, is the question -and I believe it should be considered as an aid to the municipalities, which aid would be passed on to the home owner in reduced taxation-of the sales tax on goods bought by the municipality. We have discussed this matter at some length, both in this house and elsewhere. I do not see why the federal government should tax the home owners of the township of Etobicoke $2,000 on a new fire engine which the township of Etobicoke bought and for which it paid $20,000 in order to provide the necessary protection for those homes.
An hen. Member:	Double taxation.

subsubtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think that is a case of double taxation. Perhaps it is small. Perhaps it is not as great as the others. Nevertheless it is a definite case of double taxation which I consider to be wrong and something adding again to the cost of owning and maintaining a home and family.
National Housing Act
The next point I want to mention is the question of the funded debt of the municipalities. Today municipal bonds are, by and large, bought on a 4J per cent, 5 per cent and sometimes, I presume, an even higher interest rate, possibly up to 6 per cent. I do not know of any at 6 per cent but I know of a great many at 5 per cent and 5J per cent.
What happens to the interest on the money that is lent to the municipality? The bonds are bought by individuals or by corporations and the interest goes to the individual or corporation. On that interest the individual or the corporation has to pay personal income tax or corporation income tax. Corporation taxation is about 47 per cent. Many people who buy municipal bonds are in the 50 per cent income tax bracket. This means that that bond yields the owner about 2 or 2J per cent. It yields the federal government the other 2 or 21 per cent. The home owner, however, has to pay the whole 5 per cent. Here is another case of double taxation.
The municipality must issue its debentures and its securities to yield a rate which is competitive in order that the bonds may be sold. The interest on those bonds must be paid by the home owners, through municipal taxation on property. There is only one source from which the interest on those bonds can be obtained, and that source is municipal taxation on real property. Yet the federal government, through the personal income tax and the corporation income tax, takes half the interest which the municipality must pay.
We have heard a great deal about borrowing money at 2 per cent. I do not know how it can be done in Canada, but I know how it can be done in the United States. Here again I want to make this suggestion on this whole question of housing. In the United States bonds of municipalities for improvement purposes can be and are issued free of federal taxation, so the municipal authorities in the United States can and do borrow money for from less than 2 per cent to 2J per cent. If a Canadian municipality were able to cut by half its cost of servicing its debentures, that is another way in which a saving could and would be passed on directly to the taxpayers, the owners of the houses in that municipality.
I should like to give an example of what is being done in the United States. That municipal debentures should be issued free of federal taxation is something which I think should certainly be considered here in Canada, because it does not violate any canon of banking that I know of; it seems to

National Housing Act be perfectly financially sound in the United States, and it has not caused any great financial upheaval. I want to give just one example. I obtained it out of the New York Times yesterday. It is that of the city of Durham, North Carolina, borrowing $2,225,000 for a sanitary sewer system. There are three maturities. There is one at $815,000 with a 2 per cent coupon, to yield between 1 [DOT] 4 per cent and 2 * 05 per cent. The larger one of $1,250,000 has a coupon of "l\ per cent, to yield 2-10 to 2-40 per cent. At the top of this advertisement is this notice:
Interest exempt, in the opinion of counsel, under existing laws from all federal income taxes.
The advertisement is dated January 27, 1954. We say that is a breach of our banking system. We say it is something which we have not done before, something which would be resented and objected to by the followers of the canons of sound money.
I thought I was a fair advocate of sound money, but the system under which we are operating is changing. This bill envisages as great a departure in Canadian banking as the banks going into the mortgage business. Surely if the bill envisages the banks doing this we can concede that it is not fiscally unsound for the municipalities to be given some relief, possibly the relief that is given them in the United States.
I hope the bill will be a success. Other clauses of the bill have been dealt with in great detail by members far more competent than I. But there is one thing we must preserve. When the proud parents bring the new baby from the hospital we have to remember that it is going to live for probably 20 or 21 years before going out on its own, and during that time it has to be fed, clothed and educated and has to have conveniences provided for it. The same is true of a house. It has to have provision of these essential services for 20 years at least before it becomes the outright property of its original purchasers. Every dollar which can be cut from their cost adds to the security of the owners. In my opinion the double taxation caused by the federal tax structure and regulations is the greatest destroyer of that security.

subsubtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to register my very great disappointment with the housing bill now before us. I have received considerable correspondence from my constituents also expressing disappointment with the proposals contained in the bill. I know they hoped, as many of us did, that when it was brought before the house it would make it possible for our people to build much needed housing.


When you consider the various angles of the situation and the desperate need for housing, I think everyone will agree with me that the government has failed miserably in introducing adequate proposals at this time. The preface to the bill reads as follows:
An act to promote the construction of new houses, the repair and modernization of existing houses, and the improvement of housing and living conditions.
In my opinion this legislation is a far cry from what is required to permit people in the various income brackets to build decent homes for themselves. I think it is a farce in that regard. The bill proposes to give the vested interests more security through the backing of the nation. At the same time people who will take advantage of it simply because of their desperate need for homes will be saddled with contracts the term of which has been extended from 20 to 25 or 30 years, and an interest rate which will be formidable. Later in my speech I want to document my statement that the cost to a home owner under this program will be fantastic.
I realize that each and every one of us has his own personal viewpoint on the matter of housing. I think the strength of the nation lies in its families and their homes. I believe the criterion of a good government is how it uses the total resources at its disposal, both taxes and natural resources, to raise the social and economic standards of the people. When we are facing a challenge throughout the world to what we call our free democratic system, I think it behooves us to give consideration to the most serious topic of adequate and decent houses for our people.
Today the ghosts of the hungry thirties are again rampant throughout the land. In some sections of our country we already have soup kitchens, and there are approximately 400,000 unemployed and jobless people. At the same time we have an abundance of lumber in our sawmills and lumber yards and adequate resources of every kind to build decent homes, but we find that provisions are not going to be made by the government of which the people needing homes will be able to take advantage.
As I say, each of us has his own ideas about what constitutes a decent housing program. In that connection I want to refer to the speech of the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne), which can be found at page 1417 of Hansard for January 25. In this speech he took some exception to the remarks of the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Jones) with respect to housing conditions in his constituency. The

hon. member for Kootenay East had this to say, as appears at page 1418 of Hansard:
In my opinion it is not any defect in the housing act that causes people to live in shacks, but rather the excessive cost of housing in our time.
Sir, this bill is going to make housing very expensive for our people, and I do not think the statement that the cost of houses is excessive will enable the government to relieve itself of responsibility with respect to the removing of restrictions on the cost of living some time after 1945. Further on the hon. member had this to say about the excessive cost of home ownership:
When purchasing an automobile today everyone seeks a certain amount of individuality, but in the purchase of homes people are going even farther. It would seem that every home must have its own individual design to suit the taste of the purchaser. We will either have to forget this demand for individuality or be content to pay these excessive costs.
He goes on to say:
Whether one buys a low-priced automobile or one in the $5,000 or $6,000 class he will find that, essentially, they are the same in outline, and that the differences are chiefly in the matter of colour.
First of all I want to say that I am one who does not believe it would be in the interests of our people if their houses had to be all of one type. I think it is everyone's right to have some individuality in his home.
Furthermore, in regard to automobiles, which are outside the scope of this debate, I am sure hon. members will agree that when you go into the higher priced automobiles you feel that you get more than a different colour or paint. The same holds true with regard to houses. What we are speaking of now, sir, is not the high priced home, but good homes of a decent standard for our people.
Then I should like to refer to a speech delivered by the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Dupuis) as recorded in Hansard for January 25, at page 1434. The hon. member said:
No one can seriously imply, not even my C.C.F. friends, that there might come a time when property owners who have taken advantage of this plan will lose the money they have spent because they will no longer be able to meet their obligations.
Now, gentlemen, that is easy to say, and it is very easy to appear to sympathize with the plight of the poor. But, as far back as I can remember, I have known that those who cannot meet their obligations unfortunately stand to lose, in many instances, what they have already paid. Such is the case for automobiles, electric refrigerators and so on. If the buyer is not in a position to meet his payments, he stands to lose what he has already paid. That is unfortunate, but he must accept his loss, as we all have to accept our woes, since we are all in a valley of tears, as it is so well put in a certain prayer.
I do not believe that is the sort of attitude we should have in the matter of houses. I do not believe we should have the proposition
National Housing Act
put' before hon. members of this house that people are going to have to put themselves in this position for 25 years, which is the amortization period suggested.
As I said before, sir, the incomes of many of our people are going down. I have here a report from today's Globe and Mail quoting Mr. Howard Harper in his presidential address to the Ontario soil and crop association. He said that farm income is down 16 per cent from 1949. In addition to that we have the statement that many people are in a price squeeze. This statement appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of January 26, 1954. Mr. H. H. Hannam is reported as saying that the drop in selling prices while production has remained high has placed Canada's 600,000 farm families in a price-cost squeeze which, in all likelihood, will be continued into 1954. We have the same situation all along the line. We have the jobless people and we have our farmers receiving lower incomes under present conditions.
I have here, Mr. Speaker, statistics which have been computed from figures released by the dominion bureau of statistics for 1953. I should like to place some of these on Hansard to indicate that there are many people who are not going to be able to take advantage of this bill. I think it would be of interest for me to go through the different brackets of income. First we have the grand total of those people who made out income tax returns, taxable and non-taxable, for the year 1951, of 4,102,170. There were 14.7 per cent with incomes under $1,000; 28-1 per cent with incomes between $1,000 and 2,000; 30-4 per cent with incomes between $2,000 and $3,000; 16-1 per cent with incomes between $3,000 and $4,000; 5-2 per cent with incomes between $4,000 and $5,000; 4-3 per cent with incomes between $5,000 and $10,000; 1 per cent with incomes between $10,000 and $25,000.
We found, sir, that persons with incomes under $2,000 make up 42-8 per cent of those making income tax returns. Persons with incomes under $3,000 make up 73-2 per cent of the total number making income tax returns in 1951. One can readily see from these figures that the bulk of our people are not going to be able to take advantage of this bill under any circumstances. Suppose there are some people who, out of desperation, will try to take advantage of the legislation that is proposed. When they go to the lending company they will want to buy a house. The lender will not say, "You are going to buy two houses" but that is in effect what the prospective home owner is going to have to do by the time he has paid for the house.

National Housing Act
Here is an example. On a house which has a $10,000 lending value, 90 per cent of the first $8,000 would be $7,200; that is the proposal made in the bill. Then 70 per cent of the remaining $2,000 would be $1,400, which would make a total of $8,600. If that were amortized over 25 years to compute the monthly payments, including insurance, it would mean a monthly payment of $56.13 or a total of $673.56 per year. Over a period of 25 years the home owner would have paid back, if he were that fortunate, a total of $16,839 or almost 100 per cent over the original amount of money which he borrowed. When you consider that, in addition, he would have paid his down payment, obtained the site for his house and furnished his house, you can see how far from the orbit of practicability the bill is now.
In conclusion I want to say that the bill strikes me as nothing short of a farce. I recall that in Biblical times the word "usurer" was often used in reference to these moneychangers. At the time they did not have the backing of the treasury of a great and powerful country, but today it would seem to me that is the situation. There are many safeguards for the investor, but there is no safeguard for the prospective home owner. My opinion could be summed up by saying this bill is a conglomeration of liberal mentality concocted into a capitalist bill which is going to be foisted upon an unsuspecting public. I hope that when the bill comes back from the committee we shall have something better than we have now.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the importance attached to the question of housing, more particularly by the people I represent in this house, I cannot let the debate on the housing bill end without adding my own remarks.
The first observation I wish to make has to do with the protection of the family. In fact, the most important point in this regard is to ensure, first and above all, the protection of the family and more particularly of large families. Today, large families have trouble in finding shelter, somewhat like at the time when St. Joseph was trying to find a shelter for his wife who was expecting our Saviour's birth. Large families are always turned away when they seek a dwelling and, as a result, they have to live in the slums of our large cities. Yet, in our country, as everywhere else, the family is the source of the most important asset, our human resources. I note that the present housing legislation gives private enterprise the opportunity of

*working in the public interest. I therefore hope that our large families will be able to take advantage of this legislation to improve their condition.
I would also like to say a word about small towns and villages. In the constituency I represent there are no large centres of population, but each locality wishes to do its share to ensure the future of our country. Until now, small towns and villages have not received all the attention they deserve. However, I note that banks will now be able to make mortgage loans and that it will now be possible to help our small towns and villages expand, develop and take a deeper interest in the country.
Our small towns and villages are more important than ever, because we still have, in our vast country, wide open spaces, practically uninhabited, while other not so distant districts are overpopulated, and this is particularly true in the province of Quebec where one-third of the population lives in the southern part, while, in the rest of the province, the population is very inadequately spread. Well, if our small towns and villages can contribute to the development of the country through home ownership, I am convinced that in the future they will play an important part in the development not only of our provinces but of the country as a whole. As a matter of fact, when home ownership is made easier for those who live in small towns and villages, the economic structure is strengthened in the locality, the district, the province, and throughout the country.
I am happy to note that, from now on, We shall be in a position to expect greater benefits for local communities. I am also happy to see that this legislation favours the cooperative movement in the housing field. If there is one movement to which I pay special attention, that is the one. There is no better way of helping our workers obtain accommodation in the most economical way possible.
Now as to aid to municipalities wishing to improve their housing possibilities, I notice that a whole subsection of the bill is devoted to this matter. The federal government is willing to incur 75 per cent of the charges involved in subsidizing rental housing projects. I hope that the Quebec government will finally grant to municipalities their freedom, so that they may, in future, take advantage of this legislation, in view of the fact that, to my mind and in the opinion of many others, provincial autonomy is not at all involved in this instance. In fact, this is a contract made

up for a given period of time and I hope that the Quebec provincial government will help our workers and municipalities take advantage of the benefits of this legislation.
This bill provides for the improvement of the housing situation in three ways. It provides aid at the time of purchase, it provides for the locating of and finally for the alteration of houses or existing buildings. In this way, the door is open to prospective home owners; it is open to those who, in the past, were not interested in mortgage investments, which would have helped our low-income families to become home owners, or again those who do not wish to do so but who want, however, to live at all times in suitable housing.
Thirdly, the aim is to promote the conversion of existing houses. As a matter of fact, we can see here and there in certain communities some very nice and very large houses in which only three or four persons are living but which could shelter some twenty people if their owners had the means to convert them. Thanks to this act, our home owners will be able in the future to think about increasing the number of houses in our own communities. To me, that is a very interesting way of proceeding towards the solution of this very important problem.
What is more, under this act, the down payment on an $8,000 house will be only 10 per cent. Well, I think that is one way of helping and protecting the small wage earner. I do not know if it is possible in other districts to build a house for less than $8,000, but in my own district it is quite possible to do so. Since they will have to make a down payment of only $800, our people will be able to become home owners. It is absolutely necessary that our people remain property-minded, that is sacrifice-minded.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that this act will promote throughout the country, and particularly in my district and in my constituency, the building of a sufficient number of new houses to better help the development of the Canadian family.

After all, Mr. Speaker, legislation which is designed to furnish more homes for the people of our country should have some realistic relationship to the wages earned by the people who will require these homes, and to the prospect of their being able to avail themselves of the opportunities offered by the bill.
It seems to me there are two or three things which might well be considered very seriously

in drawing up the regulations. One is the point I mentioned a few moments ago, namely, that some of these people are even now paying much more in rent than is recognized as a reasonable amount in terms of the 23 per cent limitation. Why is that? One reason is that they cannot find places in which to live without paying a great deal more than they should; another reason is, as the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) said the other day, that two, three and four members of a family are all contributing towards the cost of their housing accommodation, whatever it may be. In the case of young married couples, very often both husband and wife are working. In the case of those who have borne a family there are probably two or three children who have now reached the age where they are employed themselves. These young people within families also contribute towards the housing accommodation which they occupy, whether it be on a rental basis or whether they are attempting to buy their own home.
I submit it is only reasonable that the circumstances under which these people live should be taken into consideration. If a wage earner is in the $3,000 category, and if his wife and/or his children are supplementing the family income, then the gross amount of their earnings should be taken into consideration, particularly if these persons will agree to assume some responsibility in the matter of making payments. I can cite several cases from my own experience in which young people not yet married, and living at home, are helping their parents to liquidate the mortgage on the home. These same parents could not possibly have hoped to carry the load of home ownership without the help of their children. In turn, when these young people set up their own homes, I know they can reasonably expect to receive assistance from their parents who will still be in the earning class.
The difference between a ratio limitation of 23, 24, 25 and 26 per cent is very marked and it raises the question of the basis on which such limitations should be set. Who thought up the 23 per cent limitation in the first place? Why is it we should say 23 per cent is the proper figure upon which to base the calculation? I suppose we can all think back to the days of our youth when our parents told us we could afford to pay one week's salary for rent per month. That was the proper rent per month we could afford to pay for housing accommodation. But those days have gone. There are very few people today who are able to find living accommodation for one week's salary; and the few who
National Housing Act
do, I venture to say, are people who were probably fortunate enough to have purchased homes many years ago when they were not as expensive as they are today. They have paid off a large portion of their mortgage, and throughout the years, when they were paying off that mortgage, they probably did not have to pay 23 per cent; otherwise they could not have established themselves. Very few now are able to live in comfortable surroundings on one week's wages per month. However, as conditions change people adjust themselves to these changed conditions. They supplement their income in other ways. They cut their coat according to the cloth.
The actual difference between 23 and 24 per cent, say, at the $10,000 level is $160 in salary requirements. When you go up to the 25 per cent limitation you benefit by another $140, and when you go up to the 26 per cent you benefit by another $135. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, if it should be said that instead of the 23 per cent limitation a proper limitation was 26 per cent, you would have the advantage of about $440, which would make quite a difference in the matter of eligibility in loans under the bill.
I hope the minister will take all these things into consideration when the regulations are drawn up, because I believe very firmly that the workability of this bill when it becomes an act, and the availability of funds for housing, will depend largely upon the requirements which are written into it. I would seriously urge the minister not to block off a large majority of the wage earners of Canada from participating in a scheme which is sorely needed in order to provide homes for our people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of respect that I rise to make my contribution to the debate we have had and are having in regard to the new National Housing Act. I feel the act is a forward step in a field where the federal government is eminently suited to act, that is in the field of finance as applied to housing.
The debate has featured some criticism of the bill. We have been told that the down payments remain too high; that the monthly payments will be too high; that the proposed mortgage and salary requirements will be too high; and that even the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation standards are too high for those who wish to qualify under the bill.
With regard to these criticisms I feel and respectfully submit that certain considerations have been overlooked. First of all,

National Housing Act
all of the criticisms I have outlined basically provide for the protection of the home buyer. As to the monthly payment, based presumably on a 23 per cent ratio of the buyer's salary, it has been found, in the light of experience, and not only by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation but by all other service organizations which have occasion to study the problem, such as the social workers and so forth, that a person should not spend more than a certain proportion-23 per cent to 25 per cent-of his income on housing. This is done to protect the buyer. I have often explained this in great detail to clients whom I have faced across my desk. There is no sense of their going into that project unless there is some hope of their carrying it through. Otherwise they will lose their equity or down payment, everything they had put into the house as they proceed with the purchase of it.
It has been said by the opposition that we have no right to assume how a person will spend his money. Obviously we have no such right, but we must, of course, work on the basis of averages and we are entitled to do so in this act. I will deal with the salary requirement a little bit later.
The second point I want to make is this. There has been an assumption that the old National Housing Act, as I suppose I can now call it, has been an abject failure. Nothing could be more wrong. We should look at the operation of the old act, because the new act is obviously an attempt to extend and to better the benefits of the old act. We should look at the old act to see how it worked.
In my riding of York-Scarborough, which is part of the Toronto suburban area-I only mention it to provide an example, and it is an area which is, as the hon. member for York-Humber so aptly described it, a pulsating, growing, suburban part of Toronto- we have had an increase in population over the last year of some 18,000 people in one small area alone. Eighty per cent of the 18,000 are people who are purchasing their own homes. Of those purchasing, the vast majority have purchased homes that have been built under the National Housing Act. The National Housing Act, as it now stands, has indeed been doing a tremendous service to the home buyers of Canada and we have no right to assume that it was a failure. We have every right to expect that the extension and the betterment of the act that is contemplated will be a further boon to

the prospective home buyers. Let me give a concrete example of what can happen under this act.
I act for a builder who builds in my riding. Recently, by which I mean in the late fall of 1953, he was able to produce a home which would sell for $10,050-it was a very nice masonry home-with a down payment of $2,050 and the balance of $8,000 under a National Housing Act loan. He advertised it one evening in the Toronto Daily Star. That was on a Friday. By Monday 33 houses were sold, and we had a waiting list as long as your arm for anybody who might cancel his order. That is what happened in one day or over one week end; 33 houses sold and people clamouring to purchase more.
I dare say that if, under the new act, that builder was able to produce a home for $9,000, to sell with a down payment of $2,000 and with a $7,000 National Housing Act mortgage, the prospective home buyers in the Toronto metropolitan area, of whom there are many thousands, would literally beat a path to the builder's door. I am not at all pessimistic as to the effect of the new act. There we could use a $7,000 National Housing Act loan, where the salary requirement would not be $3,860 a year but somewhere in the neighbourhood of $3,000 a year. We have no right to assume that the minimum loan under the act will be $8,000. That is not true at all. I feel that builders will have the ability to build houses to sell for less than $10,000 under the aegis of the new act, if two conditions are fulfilled. One of those conditions is, of course, that we must have a free flow of mortgage money. The second is that there must be available serviced land on which the builder can build.
As to the free flow of mortgage money, may I say this. Housing is not merely a question of putting roofs over floors, walls and cellars. It involves a complicated process of co-ordinating the efforts of the lending institutions, the banks, the municipal governments and the provincial governments to produce, in the end, and to maintain the structure in which the buyer will live. With a free flow of mortgage money the builder, instead of having to build houses in dribs and drabs of 23 or 33 at a time, will be able to plan ahead. If he can rely on a continuous and assured flow of money, naturally his planning will be more broad; he can work on a larger scale; his costs will be reduced and his efficiency will be increased. As I say, I have no doubt that, under such conditions, a builder will be able to build good houses-even in the Toronto area where we

have costs which are probably as high as if not higher than those anywhere else in Canada-for at least $9,000. I feci that the banks can, must and will take advantage of the new legislation so that the builder will be assured of a continuous and free flow of mortgage money. Let us hope that will be the case.
What about the question of serviced land? I feel that here we have a much bigger problem. By services I mean of course the provision of roads, water, .sewers, hydro, police and fire protection and, of course, that most costly of all services, namely schools. In a subdivision of about 200 or 300 homes you need a school that costs well-nigh half a million dollars. It is an extremely expensive proposition indeed.
How is the supply of serviced land controlled and regulated? In Ontario we have what is known as a planning act. Under the planning act a municipality has the power to declare an area to be an urban development area. If it does so, land that is affected by that declaration cannot then be subdivided until a plan of subdivision is registered against the title. The plan is drawn up and is submitted to the Ontario municipal board, which sends it out to about 13 different agencies for their approval. Then, if it is approved, it is sent to the municipality concerned and the municipality must, of course, also approve the plan. This is the procedure which the subdivider and/or the builder must carry out if he is to register his plan and commence building on the property.
What happens to that plan? I am afraid I have a particular interest in the Toronto area, and that is why I speak of it; but I think what I am saying applies generally throughout the country. The plans are presented to the municipal board and they are turned down not because it is bad planning or even unreasonable planning, or even that they do not want an area to develop in a certain direction. They are turned down because the cost of the services will raise the municipal debt to such a point that there will be too great a difference between the possible assessment on the houses and the debt itself. In other words, it is wholly a problem of municipal finance.
If we are to have sufficient serviced land on which builders may construct homes and take advantage of any free flow of mortgage money that may possibly be created by this legislation, then there has to be a frontal attack on the whole sphere of municipal finance by the provincial governments. They must try to provide a more equitable distribution of municipal taxes with respect to the
National Housing Act
provision of schools, roads, and hydro, water and other required services. Otherwise our whole effort in endeavouring to put this legislation into effect may go for nothing. With this bill we are endeavouring to set the play in motion. We are commencing an attack on the so-called housing problem. Let us hope that the other agencies involved, banks, provincial governments and municipalities, will not flinch and falter when it comes to their turn to carry the ball.

If we concede that the bill
will not meet the objectives for which it was designed, and the debate makes this self-evident, then I suggest it is incumbent on the house to seek alterations which give promise of achieving the objectives. In the first place, I think the validity of the fundamental concept of the bill should be examined. It assumes that individual home ownership is almost a sine qua non. I would dispute this basic assumption. How many families in urban localities have grown up and made their contribution to society in homes that they themselves did not own? It will be found that hundreds of thousands of the very best that this country has produced lived and lived well in rented premises.
I think that the emphasis in the bill should perhaps be shifted from home ownership to low rental housing. Mind you, I have no objection to the principle of home ownership. I would not favour altering the bill in any
rMr. Trainor.]
respect with regard to this principle. The bill provides for home ownership for certain groups of people. There is nothing wrong with individual ownership except that it is designed for those who wish it and, more particularly, for those who can afford it.
We shall have to concede that normal investment funds are not available for low rental housing largely because the return is too low and the conditions too uncertain to attract investment capital. Therefore I submit it is necessary to seek another agency. In this regard I should like to suggest to the minister that business and industry have the necessary social consciousness and sense of social responsibility to assume the burden of providing suitable housing for their own employees at a price they can afford to pay, provided, however, that this is not added to their operating expenses and consequently reflected in the price structure.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is definitely in the interests of industry and business, because obviously the welfare of their employees must be of interest to them. The bill provides also, in a limited way, for this sort of participation by industry by specifying the industries of mining, lumbering, logging and so forth. Why not enlarge this provision to embrace all industry? There would be no particular objection that I can see to doing this. As a matter of fact, it would be a great social experiment.
I can envisage, Mr. Speaker, the emergence of a new social pattern wherein industry and business would gladly assume the responsibility for providing decent housing for its own employees. Such a development would unquestionably be in the best interests of business, and being based on self-interest it would be guaranteed a successful operation. I would suggest that these funds be lent to industry by the corporation when, in the judgment of the corporation, it is evident that the applicant possesses the financial stability to insure the servicing of the loan over a considerable period of time, and of course with adequate safeguards as to the rate of rental and so on.
I should say that this suggestion is entirely my own. I assume full responsibility for it, although I believe it is in accordance with the political principles of the official opposition. I offer it to the minister free and without expectation of any credit, because I believe I see in it the germ of a new social experiment which would provide decent homes for thousands of our people which this bill, in its present form, does not provide. Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the population of the county

which it is my privilege and responsibility to represent in this house, I readily support the bill now before us, the principle of which is merely in accord with the constant desire of the government to create for the Canadian people an atmosphere of security and welfare.
The administration of public affairs is a very intricate matter. However, in studying this matter more thoroughly and more objectively one notes that the things that seemed obscure, even mysterious, become clearer and more definite. Accordingly, a government conscious of its responsibilities and anxious to provide a sound administration for the people must take into account a certain number of factors which may be summarized as follows:
1.	To place upon our statute books laws which meet the highest aspirations of the people, from the moral, national, international and economic points of view and to take the necessary measures to ensure that these laws will be strictly enforced.
2.	To show decency and judgment in the spending of public moneys.
In my opinion, those are the two great factors which a serious, honest and responsible administration should bear in mind. Mr. Speaker, I am satisfied that the government to which I have the honour of belonging at the present time take those factors into account, even scrupulously, whenever they make an administrative decision. Besides, the confidence shown by the Canadian people on so many occasions, was so clear, definite and unequivocal, more particularly in 1949 and 1953, that I do not feel it is necessary to comment further on the matter.
The present leader of the government, whom all men of good will in our country, and throughout the world, take pleasure in recognizing as the principal initiator of the North Atlantic pact, a pact I would qualify as "the greatest co-operative movement for peace in the whole world", once said that, in order to fight more successfully the pernicious and subversive ideas prevalent throughout the world, it was necessary for every member nation to take steps, within its own territory, to ensure more security, welfare and prosperity for all classes of society. Well, Mr. Speaker, once the hon. members of this house and of the Senate have enacted this bill, there will be a new law on our statute books, a humanitarian, social and eminently helpful piece of legislation, because the people of our own country will thus have an additional weapon with which to fight the communist doctrine, sym-
National Housing Act
bolic of the worst degradation of the human mind, which I still call a hideous octopus trying to infiltrate into our hearts and minds its fiendish tentacles in an effort to annihilate the best asset we possess in this country: our religious convictions, our way of thinking, our way of life, and our democratic principles. Moreover, this piece of legislation will enable a great many families to house themselves properly, a great number of Canadians to become home owners. Thus, a deeper sense of private ownership will develop in the individual, and our community spirit will grow at the same time as our love for Canada.
It is for those few reasons, Mr. Speaker, that I wholeheartedly support the principle as well as the terms of the bill before us. Since then, in my constituency, hundreds of houses have been built, large families have come in and have succeeded in finding adequate housing. Thanks to the minister's efforts, I have every reason to believe that during 1954 the constituency which I have the honour to represent will continue its expansion in the field of housing.
