Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to delay the house for long at this time, but I want to deal particularly with one point which I would ask the minister and the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to look into. What I have in mind is a problem which confronts particularly the smaller municipalities which, thus far, have not been dealt with adequately. That is my main purpose in rising.
Before coming to that, however, I should like to say that I support the points made by speakers in the official opposition who have dealt with this bill, and would express the hope that the arguments and considerations they have placed before the minister and the house would receive most thoroughgoing and careful consideration.
In that connection it occurred to me that the fresh viewpoint put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Trainor) was one that arrested attention and is deserving of serious study. As I understood him, the hon. member did not question the

National Housing Act
desirability of home ownership but said he felt that not all people in Canada wanted to own their homes. He pointed out that there is a considerable group whose needs would be met quite adequately by rental housing- in fact whose needs would be met better by the provision of rental accommodation than by the provision of accommodation available only on a purchase basis.
Then, if I understood him correctly, he went on to say that he felt perhaps there was not sufficient emphasis being placed on the provision of rental accommodation, and that attention was being directed almost exclusively to the provision of accommodation for purposes of purchase and ownership. He suggested that it behooved us to devote a great deal more attention to the problems of those whose particular requirements would best be met by rental accommodation.
If I understood correctly what he said in that regard, then I support fully his point of view. I liked, too, his suggestion that, inasmuch as the returns now available from money invested in this type of accommodation were not sufficiently attractive to produce large amounts of private money for that purpose, the role of government and of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, as well as of the act, should be paramount in this field. He added that greater facilities are necessary along these lines.
I was particularly struck by his suggestion that in this field industry and business should be invited to participate, on the basis that they have a common interest and a common duty, along with the rest of the community and with the government, to see that adequate housing accommodation is furnished for those people who find employment in business and industry. I understood his suggestion to be that we might make funds available under the terms of the National Housing Act for the construction of such rental housing projects in which arrangements industry and business would participate. They would organize and take some administrative responsibility under the plan, thus making it possible to have low rental housing accommodation available for their employees. I do feel it is a matter in which business and industry should and would be willing to accept their fair share of responsibility provided, as the hon. member said-and 1 agree -that the cost of that program is not added to the overhead of business, thus increasing the prices of their products.
I think it would be possible to find ways under the rental accommodation provisions of the National Housing Act to work out such a program, in which the co-operation of

business and industry would be invited. I support fully the hon. member's suggestion that the minister and his officials should study the problem from that point of view, to find if a program along those lines could be worked out and put into effect. The hon. member, who is a new member in the house, deserves great credit for having put forward in this, his first session, this concrete suggestion, and one which, in all its implications, is fresh. What he has said should be considered as at least a partial solution of the tremendous problem of providing housing accommodation that now confronts this nation.
There can be no doubt that the problem of providing housing is one of the most serious confronting us. I need not rehearse all that has been said in that regard. I think more particularly, as I suppose all hon. members do, of the situation in my own constituency where even at this time families are living in accommodation which was provided for other purposes, and eight or nine years ago taken over on an emergency basis. After the war people were placed in that accommodation on the assumption that it would be used only as emergency shelter. They are still there, and living under conditions which are simply not good enough for Canadian people in these days.
I am not going to go into detail. I am sure many hon. members have in their constituencies so-called emergency shelter accommodation, consisting of-well, almost tarpaper shacks-temporary huts, erected on airports or adjacent to airports or army camps. This was never intended to be used as permanent dwelling accommodation. In it there are only plywood partitions to separate one end of the building from the other and to afford some measure of privacy for the occupants. Well, those of us who served as members of the armed forces during the war lived in some of those huts with plywood partitions, and we know exactly how much privacy there can be behind a plywood wall.
When one thinks of families having to dwell under those conditions, having to share bathroom facilities designed for occupancy by a group of men, such as would be found in army barracks, and realizes that this kind of accommodation is now being shared by women and children as well, one must conclude that it just is not decent in a country having the material prosperity and the potential living standards of ours.
That is what I have in mind when I say that there is no more important problem facing the country today than the necessity of

the provision of decent housing accommodation. That necessity is just as acute in the smaller centres as it is in the larger ones. I suppose it is natural that the needs of the big cities in this respect should be more emphasized in a discussion of this sort, because there are more people living in the big cities than in the smaller towns. But I am quite sure there is not a single member here from a rural area, and I doubt whether there is a member here from the cities, who would not agree with me when I say that in proportion to our population the need of housing accommodation is just as acute in the smaller centres as it is in the large ones.
I come from a riding in which there is no large city. Our biggest city, with its neighbouring municipality of North Kamloops and the immediately surrounding areas, has a population of probably 12,000 to 14,000 people. That is the biggest centre in my riding. The others are towns and villages of from about 600 to 3,000 people, and the rest of it is entirely rural. But in those smaller centres the need of accommodation is just as acute as it is in the larger centres in proportion to the population ratios that prevail between the two.
There has been brought to my attention the fact that, particularly in the smaller towns and villages, the facilities of the National Housing Act, as it stands at the present time, are not as fully available as they are in the larger centres of population. I suppose that would be natural if one considered only the facilities for inspection and the speedy arrangement of loans and so on. One could perhaps be reconciled to expecting that the processing of an application for a loan from a smaller centre would take longer than it would in a large centre where inspection and processing facilities are all immediately available. But it is not from that point of view that the criticism is directed. I am informed that in some of those smaller centres the down payment is substantially greater than what is required in the larger centres. I have figures given me from the village of Williams Lake, which is one of the typical centres of population in my riding. May I put it this way. A gentleman made a thorough study of what arrangements could be made to obtain building loans under the National Housing Act, and was informed that the minimum down payment required would be 30 per cent, not the 20 per cent which is available under the present act to those in larger centres. I am also informed that at the time this study was made 17 people indicated that they were prepared to
National Housing Act
take loans and go ahead under the National Housing Act, but when they were informed the down payment required would be 30 per cent not one of them went ahead with his application.
I understand the reason given as to why a higher down payment was required was that there was no industry located in the town in question. Well, of course, on that point I would most certainly take strong objection to that being used as a reason for requiring a higher down payment in a smaller centre. I would say that the difference in security, the risk, both moral and physical, as between property in big towns or cities and small towns, from that point of view, is so negligible that it does not form the basis of a difference in down payment of 10 per cent. In fact I would say that the moral risk is somewhat better in smaller communities than in larger ones. Certainly it is just as good, and in a good many respects the personal security involved is more satisfactory because there is not such a change in population in smaller centres, or shifts of population, as there are in the larger centres. As far as the application of any such argument to the actual village in question-Williams Lake-is concerned, I would point out that it is a very substantial distribution point, serving a large area, and that although it is true there are no heavy industries, no manufacturing industries in that area, with the exception of saw mills, its standard of income compares favourably to what it would be if the whole population were dependent upon industry itself.
I am further told, Mr. Speaker, that even the 30 per cent down payment was not quite all that these people would be expected to put up. In fact it was indicated that the home builder there would have to put down 40 per cent of the total cost, and that the nigger in the woodpile was the provision that the down payment was a minimum one, and that apparently there is some discretion to the corporation to increase that down payment in cases where it considers it necessary.
I am not familiar with all the details of the regulations and the application of the legislation, but I am putting this forward as a statement made to me by responsible people of this place after what I am satisfied was a thorough investigation. I do not know the reasons why the conditions that they report to me should exist, but I am putting it before the minister as a condition which is most serious from the point of view of smaller centres, and which places them at a

very grave disadvantage in comparison with larger centres in obtaining loans under the National Housing Act.
As I said, I am quite certain that no one living in a smaller centre, and being a reasonable person, would expect them to be equal in all respects; and the difficulties of administering it in smaller centres might create some obstacles, and would be expected to make it slightly more difficult for them to obtain the same treatment as they do in larger centres. But this tremendous disparity is not justified and, I am quite certain, not necessary. Therefore I would ask the minister to take a look at the matter himself and to have the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation take a look at the situation, because I am quite certain that it is not necessary that such discrepancy should continue. I would also ask him to take a look at the situation with regard to the inspection facilities and other facilities which it is intended to provide to smaller centres in dealing with such applications for loans as may be approved.
The minister has implied that 4,000 branches of the chartered banks of Canada may well become lending offices under the new National Housing Act, in which case of course there would be a lending office in every community where there is a branch of a bank, so that even although in the past the lending companies, which have been confined pretty well to the life insurance companies, have not made loans in smaller centres because they have not had offices there and no inspection facilities there, I suppose it might well be that if in fact the branch banks are authorized to make loans for housing purposes there will be a lending office right there. I rather doubt-and here I agree with the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming)- whether, particularly in its initial stages at any rate, the banks will authorize every one of their branches to be a lending office and to approve and process loans right there. Therefore, it seems to me, there will still be a very real need for providing adequate inspecting, lending and negotiating facilities for these smaller communities, and I would ask the minister to bear that problem in mind and, by changing the regulations under this act, or by amending the legislation itself in this connection, to eliminate this difference in the down payment required, so that, so far as is possible, reasonable, and consistent, smaller communities are placed in no less advantageous a position than big communities in getting loans for house building under the National Housing Act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened for quite a long time to this

debate and there are a few remarks I should like to make though I do not wish to take up very much time of the house.
I would like to remind hon. members that this housing situation over a period of approximately twenty years has gradually been shifted from the place where the legislative jurisdiction lies to the place where there is no legislative jurisdiction. The proper place for housing and exclusive legislative jurisdiction is in the province; it always has been and always will be, I presume. But gradually, because of a state of national housing emergency, the federal government has stepped into a field which is not properly its own, but which it was forced to step into because of national needs.
Housing has gradually become in the public mind synonymous with Ottawa. I might just remind hon. members that all we can do to assist in housing is to give financial assistance. We have no legislative jurisdiction over land, property or civil rights. If we had jurisdiction over property, particularly land, we would be in a very different position in regard to the former section 35 of the act relating to land assembly. Unfortunately, in my own province of Ontario the provincial government, which has that legislative jurisdiction, has taken very little interest in the problem of land assembly. I bring that up because today everyone we talk to about housing feels that this is our job, that it is Ottawa's job and the job of the federal government. I suppose we must admit that in a sense it is our job because we have taken the responsibility and have done the work.
Our expanding economy and expanding population can, I think, be compared somewhat to a small or a new company. When a new company is formed in a period of expansion it always finds itself undercapitalized. That is our situation today in Canada. We are a new nation expanding very rapidly and to an extent at least we are undercapitalized. There is really not quite enough money to go around and do all the things we are trying to do in this country and we have to make some arrangement whereby certain amounts will flow into certain fields for certain purposes and other amounts will flow into other fields.
It has become quite obvious in the last few years that in so far as housing is concerned we do not have enough money available. There was not sufficient money available for the borrowing public to build sufficient houses, though that of course is the

National Housing Act

It is to be hoped that by allowing the banks to enter this field under the particular circumstances designated in the bill more money will become available. speechtext:
Yes, which obviously means 25 per cent less loans from the former lending institutions.
Extending the terms of repayment reduces the down payment to some extent. The question as to what is the proper percentage for down payment will never be satisfactorily answered because there are very different views on that point. There always have been and probably always will be though I think views will change when the lending institutions realize that this country is able to produce a stability of economy and can keep away from these former depressions which we suffered in the past, or at least we are all hoping we can keep away from them. That in turn is bound to be of some psychological significance to the lender over a period of years. At the present time the lending institutions or the lenders still remember that we had a bad depression, and they still remember that during that depression values dropped drastically, and that unless a person had a sizeable stake in a house or a sizeable investment in his home he was very liable to say: "I have lost my investment and I will just clear out". That is what happened in many cases during the depression.
If it be true that by the expansion and contraction of credits and by maintaining our exports we are able to produce a stable economy, then it is quite obvious that this is going to have a psychological effect on lenders generally over a period of years and they may then be willing to take smaller down payments.
Many people today say that they should be able to obtain loans on much smaller down payments, say of $1,000. That may be their view, and maybe it is correct, but the point is that the people who are lending the money are not lending their own money but that of policyholders and depositors and they have to take a fairly conservative point of view.
I have heard a number of speeches in which hon. members have estimated the housing shortage in this country. But again I would' remind hon. members, as I did last year, that these estimates are very difficult to arrive at with any accuracy. The only possible estimate is on the act as it stands at the present time. Under the law under which we are operating at the present time, what is the measuring rod by which we estimate how many real purchasers we have in this country? How many people are really in a position to buy a house under the present law? As the law is changed you may find more people in a position to buy houses, but it is quite obvious that the only possible estimate that can be considered accurate is how many people under the present situation and under the present law are in a position to go out and buy a house, and how many of them are going to buy houses. Many people might like to buy a house but they are not in a position to pay for it and therefore they cannot be considered' under the head of housing shortage. They must be in a position to pay for a house and wish to buy. In regard to these estimates I have the gravest suspicion because I know how difficult it would be to get information which would be really accurate on the subject.
The question of the interest rate is something with which, I suppose, people will never be really satisfied. It is quite clear that unless you make the rate of interest reasonably attractive the lenders are not going to make loans. They will simply put their money into another field where the rate of interest is sufficiently attractive. The only way around that is to start subsidizing the lenders and as soon as you start that you are running into the question of discrimination, because those who are going to get the benefit of these loans will in effect be subsidized by taxpayers' money and obtaining a favour which has not been available to those who already are buying their own homes and are paying on an economic basis. I think that such action would' cause deep resentment throughout the country and I for one would not want to see it because it would cost the taxpayers a very large sum of money. You cannot manufacture a lower rate of interest. Somebody has to pay for it. As money becomes cheap the rate of interest will go down but that will depend on whether money ever does become cheap.

National Housing Act
Another thing I was interested in was the accusation that in this bill there was a centralization of power. I think that statement has some merit. Certainly there is a centralization of power. I do not see how you can have it otherwise. It is quite true that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are going to have the task of administering the bill and working with the bank and they are going to have to pass judgment on the loans made by the bank, because the lender is simply going to send the application over to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for its report and valuation, and' if it is accepted and the report is favourable and the borrower wishes to go ahead that would be the final valuation. The lending value would be apparent, and the administration will go on through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
So in that sense there is no question about it that there is a concentration of administration there. The whole question is this. What alternative would you have? If we are going to get the banks into this thing, it is quite clear at this point that they are not in a position to enter into the mortgage business and to establish mortgage departments on their own. Good mortgage men are extremely scarce. The banks have not had sufficient experience to enter into that field. If we forced them to do the administration of this business, we would be in the position, I am afraid, where we would get very few loans for a long time from the banks. Therefore the 'only logical way of doing it was to let Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation do this administrative work. That could be the subject of some criticism.
I think the main thing we have to bear in mind and which I think the officers of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will have to bear in mind-as I know they are bearing it in mind-is the efficiency of their administration. If these loans in any way get bogged down with red tape, it is going to be a source of irritation to the borrowing public, or the people seeking housing, and a tremendous source of irritation to the builders; and the builders are, generally speaking, the people who produce most of the housing. Builders have a tendency to dislike anything like Central Mortgage anyway, because Central Mortgage has a number of regulations which are made in an effort to produce good housing. No builder wants to be curtailed any more than is necessary. He naturally wants to get into the field, build as many houses 'as he can and sell them as quickly as he can for as much profit as possible. Any interference


by Central Mortgage would naturally be resented by the builder because it might possibly diminish his profit and it might cause him to do a great many things which he might not otherwise do. But that cannot be helped. In our free enterprise, we like to keep it free but it cannot be so free that we are not getting good houses.
I think that Central Mortgage is a highly necessary organization. I think it is run efficiently. I think that is true to date and we hope it will be so in the future. If Central Mortgage is able to provide efficiency of administration for these new loans, I think we are going to see a development in the lending field such as we hardly even expect at this time. I think we will see a tremendous amount of lending for housing. I am hoping indeed that we can meet the needs of the public of this country to a much greater degree. I think that this act is a splendid step forward. It is progressive. It is going to do a task that is highly necessary. Possibly it should have come a little bit earlier. Who is to say? It is difficult to do this sort of thing because you cannot, just overnight, order people to lend money. You have to get them to agree to it. You have to have their co-operation. Until you have their co-operation, you are not able just suddenly to put something on the statute books and say, "This is the way it will go". Until you have had preliminary discussions with the banks and the lending institutions generally and have worked out some system which is agreeable to them, and which they will accept-it may not be the final system and it may not be the best system in the end but it is the one that you can put into force at the present time-you are not in a position to enter into a new field of legislation.
These agreements have been worked out. The new legislation has been introduced. I think it will do an excellent job. I do not think it is the end of this thing. I think as public opinion veers and varies, and as the lending institutions realize what is happening in this field, we shall find coming along amendments which in time may produce more and better housing yet. But under the present set-up and under the present psychology of the lending public, I think this act is a magnificent step forward. I must say that to the minister and to the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation I extend my sincere and genuine congratulations.

I wish, then, to offer with regard to this bill a few suggestions which, to my mind, would be such as to correct this serious situation.
I am in favour of the immediate establishment of federal grants for building materials, in the proportion of 90 per cent. Let there be no misunderstanding in this regard: these grants would necessarily be converted into mortgages.
Middle class people having but a small amount to pay for their materials would then be in a position to carry out the building of their house with the co-operation of relatives and friends.
In the suburbs of Quebec, several workers have already taken advantage of this suggestion, so that they have been able to build themselves, for about $8,000, a most adequate duplex from which they will be able to earn fairly substantial revenue. In this way, with a lot acquired through their own sacrifices and about $1,000 down payment, a large number of workers will be able to become happy home owners, without having to assume an indebtedness of $10,000 which they would not be in a position to clear before 25 or 30 years.
Why not also provide in the act some measure of help for those who, at the present time, are bearing the burden of a heavy debt because they wanted to have a house of their own?
Would it not be possible, under this legislation, to have the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation take over certain mortgages already existing with several insurance companies or lending institutions and which have to be repaid within 10 or 15 years? Let me give an example. Here is a workingman who has saved enough money for a down payment on a house and for the land on which to build that house. However, he had to borrow $8,500 from an insurance company, and he has to repay that loan over a period of ten years. The insurance people have made him buy from them an insurance policy as security for the mortgage to the amount of $5,000, and the borrower must pay each month a $12 premium. This worker is

then obliged to make monthly payments of about $107. To this must be added municipal taxes amounting to $450 per year, $200 for heating and the upkeep of the said property.
How can anyone expect that this worker will not get discouraged or that he would not be in danger, in case of illness or unemployment, of losing the savings which have cost him so much work and such heavy sacrifices.
I hope that the government whose responsibility it is to legislate for the people will consent to make, in the bill we are now asked to approve, the changes that are required if the government really cares to help those who are in need of such help. If we do this, we will then have found, as I have already said, one of the most efficient means of fighting the subversive ideas which are much too often bred in the slums and the distressed homes I mentioned earlier.
Democracy should not be an empty word nor a matter for propaganda in parliament. It must really exist. Let us legislate for the people if we want our people to have, towards our parliamentary institutions, the respect they deserve.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first chance I have had to discuss housing since the minister has become responsible for this important branch of government. While I plan on making some critical remarks regarding the proposal before the house, I should like to say that members of this group will be supporting the measure, because it will provide some housing. It will be better than no legislation at all. But I really do not think it is good enough for Canada in this day and generation.
I would like to express my sympathy to the minister. I feel that, being well qualified as he is in engineering, and with his vision
National Housing Act
for the future, his colleagues in the cabinet are taking advantage of his youth and his good nature by having him sponsor a bill of this type.
When one considers the performance by Canada during the war years alongside our record in housing since the war, I think he cannot be satisfied. It is just ten years ago since the well-known Curtis report was presented. That was on March 24, 1944. I think it would be well for us to remember something of the plans for the brave new world that was to dawn as soon as the war was over.
This committee summarized its findings by pointing out the following:
Canada has lagged behind the example of European countries, of Great Britain and the United States in providing greater governmental assistance for housing as a matter of welfare and public concern. These substantial reasons put housing into the forefront of domestic post-war plans. The subcommittee believes that the provision for housing will have to include home ownership, home improvement, slum clearance, low rental projects and rural and farm housing.
And later on it says:
It seems indicated that special attention in the advance preparation of plans should be given to low rental housing and farm housing, in which this country has had little or no experience to date; and also that home and farm improvement should be made ready the most urgently in advance, because of its immediate applicability to the first period of demobilization . . . The committee places in the forefront of all housing projects the matter of town and community planning. Town planning is essentially the matter of using land in its most efficient and socially desirable way. Many people regard town planning as a matter of parkways, arterial roads, and similar measures. But town planning should mean the utilization of all land in terms of long-range and carefully considered objectives. Obviously, this process must extend beyond the more or less arbitrary boundaries of our present cities and unite with organized rural planning wherever appropriate. The institution of at least the essentials of town planning is both preliminary and basic to housing developments. The committee, therefore, regards it as a step which must be taken at the earliest possible moment in preparation for post-war housing projects;-
And so on. The two points stressed by the committee as requiring top priority were low rental subsidized housing and rural housing. Some of my colleagues in this party have discussed the question of low rental subsidized housing, and I do not propose to go over the ground that they have covered sa well. But I do wish to say that it has been a well-established principle in all countries that the community pays a very high price for maintaining run-down slum areas in our large cities. It has been a false economy for Canada through many years to fail to deal with this question.
I know we have made a start. But, again, when we compare the performance of this

National Housing Act
country during the war, when millions of our young people were in the services and when we were supplying munitions for our army as well as those of our allies, with the pitiful performance since the war in tearing down and burning these disgraceful slums found in every large centre of Canada, what we have done is not so impressive, and we cannot be satisfied with it.
I hope the minister sponsoring the bill will bring in legislation next year and every year to indicate that he is making some progress with the cabinet in getting that measure of support which would ensure that the federal government would lead the way, in co-operation with the provinces and municipalities, in the provision of low rental housing. This would be subsidized, of course, to make it possible for those people in the lower income brackets to have decent houses.
I think it is only fair that when a country is making heavy appropriations for the building of large industrial plants, at the same time adequate provision should be made to provide living quarters for the people who work in those plants.
When the debate opened a week ago today I was on my way to Uranium City and Eldorado. It was 62 degrees below zero the day we reached Eldorado, and it gave me pleasure to note that the federal crown-owned corporation did not expect the people working for it in the far north to rustle logs to build log shacks. Excellent living quarters have been provided for the people working on that northern project.
When in all parts of Canada large expenditures, into the millions, are being made to provide new equipment and plants, either the companies building the plants or some government organization, whether municipal, provincial or federal, should see that comfortable living quarters are made available for those working in the plants.
The present legislation is open to criticism therefore because it does not make adequate plans for the clearing of slums in the cities [DOT]of this country. Looking through the speeches of hon. members who have taken part in the debate I have found very little comment concerning rural housing. I cannot accuse the government of ignoring the problem completely. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has issued a publication known as "Housing In Canada", which purports to be a factual summary for the third quarter of 1953. I find in it information about housing operations conducted by a number of branches of government.
For instance, I find that under the Veterans Land Act houses have been provided for

some people who might be regarded as living in rural areas. Then, under the Canadian Farm Loan Act I find that loans were issued for new structures as follows:
New Structures;
Year	Number of Loans
1945		 53
1946		 57
1948		 62
1949		 86
1950		 71
1951		  64
Then, I have figures to show the building of new structures under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. They are as follows:
New Structures;
Year	Number of Loans
1945		 232
1946		 375
1947		 387
Then there is another table setting out the number of farm units in Canada on which the gross mortgage loans on real estate have been approved by lending institutions. This information is given having relation to the type of loan. The table indicates that in
1947 the number of loans on farms stood at 1,704, while in 1948 it was 1,738. The year
1948	was the big year. Since then there has been a drop. In 1949 it was 1,579; 1950, 1,550; 1951, 1,368; and in 1952 it had fallen to 1,170. That is a start, Mr. Speaker, but certainly it is not a very impressive performance.
May I refer again to the Curtis report. It visualized a post-war housing program that would result in 100,000 farm units being built. It referred to the deplorable housing conditions on the farms in all provinces in Canada. In the report of the Curtis committee, I find there is a table giving the percentage of the farm houses of the various provinces without bathing facilities. The figures are as follows: Prince Edward Island, 93 per cent; Nova Scotia, 91-4 per cent; New Brunswick, 93-0 per cent; Quebec, 93-2 per cent; Ontario, 89-3 per cent; Manitoba, 96-8 per cent; Saskatchewan, 96 [DOT] 1 per cent; Alberta, 95 [DOT] 7 per cent; British Columbia, 76.5 per cent. Without flush toilets, 91 [DOT] 9 per cent of the farm homes in Canada were without these facilities in 1941, prior to the writing of the Curtis report.
Some of the suggestions made at that time should have received sympathetic consideration from the minister in charge of this department. The report says:
The wisest course would seem to be the setting up either of a special rural division of the national housing administration, or at least a farm housing advisory committee which would include representatives from the Department of Agriculture. This procedure would not be incompatible with the existence of a rural housing committee within the Department of Agriculture, which might give special attention to housing and other farm facilities in their broader relations to agricultural efficiency.

I checked with the bureau of statistics to see whether they had information from the 1951 census on rural housing conditions according to federal constituencies, but they informed me that the information is not being compiled in that way; now it is being compiled on the census divisions. Therefore the last statistics that are available with respect to my own constituency are the 1941 census which gives interesting information. The value of the owner-occupied dwellings on the farms-these are the valuations placed by the farmer himself and by the census taker, who was a neighbour-are as follows. These are 1941 figures. The C.C.F. government in Saskatchewan does not take the credit or the blame. These are the figures: $656 for the farm and $813 for the non-farm. I am not suggesting that there are not houses that are worth a good deal more than that, but they appear to be the average values on the sample that was used when the census was being taken. Houses needing external repairs amounted to 42-2 per cent in the country and 34-4 per cent in the villages; houses that had furnace heating numbered 2-4 per cent; houses that had running water, * 1 per cent, just one out of a thousand. Apparently there were not enough flush toilets on the farms in Mackenzie to warrant an entry. There is a blank here. Number of houses with electric lights, 1 [DOT] 7 per cent; refrigeration, ice or mechanical, 3 * 8 per cent; radios, 52 * 3 per cent; automobiles, 25-2 per cent; telephones, 13-9 per cent; and one person out of a thousand had vacuum cleaners. It is pretty obvious that with that sort of housing available in the rural parts of Canada there is a field here in which the government of today should have been making ambitious plans, to make sure that the rural standards should be brought up to the standards found in our cities.
Reports from government agencies now indicate that we have a recession. Whether it is a major or a minor recession remains to be seen, but the number of persons unemployed in Canada at the moment apparently is higher than it has been at any time since the war. It should be pretty obvious that an ambitious housing program would be one of the finest projects that the government could undertake. If we could carry out the suggestions made in the Curtis report, that we wipe out the slums and embark on a low-rental subsidized housing program and solve the rural housing problem in Canada, there would be employment for carpenters, plumbers, tinsmiths and plasterers. There would be a market for a very large volume of building
National Housing Act
materials. That would be one way that Canada might avoid the effects of mass unemployment that we had in the 1930's. Therefore, I submit, the minister should give careful consideration to the suggestions which have come from this side of the house, and before the bill comes back for third reading incorporate these suggestions in it.
I was interested in a paragraph in the memorandum submitted to the government by the Canadian Congress of Labour on December 10. They drew attention to the fact that the speech from the throne promised:
. . . measures to increase and broaden the supply of mortgage money so that more people with moderate incomes will be able to find facilities to enable them to build their own homes. This is welcome information, but it does not get to the root of the problem. Helping people with "moderate incomes" is no doubt desirable. But helping people with low incomes is even more desirable, and much more urgent.
I regret very much that the minister has not made provision for a housing program that would make houses available for people in the low-income brackets. In conclusion I should like to endorse the proposals presented by my colleague, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), that the federal government should undertake to make money available for housing at 2 per cent. My neighbour, the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Trainor), was critical of this proposal, but interest rates are determined by government policies. No one can deny the fact that investment in housing for the Canadian people would be a safe investment that should not require any higher interest than 2 per cent. The amortization period should be extended to 30 years.
When my wife and I set up housekeeping some 24 years ago we built a house, and I am quite sure that that house, after it has been used for 24 years, would sell for a good deal more than it cost 24 years ago. It is of frame construction. If it had been built of brick or stone the life would be longer; but, certainly in our part of Canada, a frame house that is kept painted can be expected to last for 40 or 50 years, and still be quite liveable. Therefore, having the house amortized over a period of 30 years is not unreasonable. The loans should be 90 per cent of the lending value. That is also reasonable. There are a great many people in Canada who want to own their own homes, and they could pay for their homes if given a start. The government of this country should take a chance on giving them a loan up to 90 per cent of the maximum lending value of $12,000. The government should

National Housing Act also have something to say on the very large quantities of building materials that are now going into theatres, bowling alleys, hotels, and other places of recreation. The building materials that are available should be used to a greater extent in providing houses for people of moderate incomes and those in the lower income brackets as well. I hope the minister will give most careful consideration to these suggestions and incorporate them in his bill.

Mr. Speaker, the house may take some comfort from the fact that I am not going to make a speech but merely rise at this time to ask a question. It arises from the minister's statement on December 16 where he said, as reported at page 999 of Hansard:
However, it is proposed that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation shall continue to make loans to limited dividend companies and companies engaged in primary industries-
This is the part I am concerned with.
-and, under some circumstances, to persons who are unable to secure loans from approved lenders.
These are the people with whom, it seems to me, most of us as members come in contact, those persons who for some reason or another, perhaps on grounds of a mere technicality, may not qualify and will be unable to get their loans from approved lending institutions.


The minister may recall that a couple of years ago when building bogged down in northern Ontario under the joint loan plan, I recommended at that time that the government proceed with the direct loan phase of the legislation, and it was some time after that that the regulations were changed, and in areas containing a population greater than 5,000 these direct loans were made. From my personal experience in the north, and I speak only from personal experience, that was the only thing which did assist in getting more houses built. I would like to ask the minister if he would tell the house the amount of loans made in 1953 under this direct loan phase, and I would like to know if it is the government's policy to expand or restrict this phase, because I certainly believe the government through the corporation should stand ready to make such direct loans in substantial volume where necessary and where the approved lending institutions fail to do so.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member
for Wentworth (Mr. Lennard), I believe that nearly everything that can be said on this bill has already been said. However, since I come from a population centre of Canada where the housing situation is bad and has been bad for a long time, it might be considered strange if I did not say something in this debate.
I believe I am speaking for all the members of the C.C.F. group when I say that while we feel there are many grave shortcomings in this bill we are going to vote for it because we believe it is an effort to meet the present situation, although we believe it is not being met in the way it should be. I believe the government will have to give more attention to the building of low rental homes, because some people will never be able to get sufficient money in advance for a down payment, and these people, may I add, are paying exorbitant rents now for very inferior accommodation. But there is also the fact that in a city like Vancouver there are many people for whom the ownership of a home would be a liability. These are the people who have no steady employment in one place. They are here for a couple of months and somewhere else for the next couple of months, and then they travel somewhere else after that. Anyone can understand that a home for such people, and there are a great many people in my province in seasonal employment, even if they could afford a down payment and afford to buy a home, would be a liability. They must always be in a position where, as soon

as one job finishes, they can pull up stakes and move to the locality where the next job may be.
I am therefore convinced the government will have to give more attention to the building of low rental homes because private enterprise will not provide that kind of accommodation. As a matter of fact, I was rather surprised to hear one of the members on my right criticize the government for going too far in the housing business, and to hear it claimed that the prospects should be made more attractive to private enterprise.
I want to tell this house, Mr. Speaker, that private enterprise has never yet anywhere in any country provided housing for those who need housing most.
My first view of the older countries of Europe was in connection with the slums in which the working class of those countries lived, and I compared that with the splendor in which royalty and the owning class lived. That is the picture in every country in the world where governments have not concerned themselves with providing housing accommodation. In this new and rich country the growing slum conditions in every big city is proof positive that private enterprise cannot provide homes for those who need them most.
While we are going to vote for this bill we are quite satisfied it will no more meet the situation that confronts the people of Canada in the matter of housing than the various housing acts that have gone before. That is all I wish to say. I hope the genial Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) will pay attention to what I have said, not because I have said it but because it is a correct picture of things as they are.

These villages are all growing in size; they are getting larger every day. Better houses would and could be built if direct loans could and would be given by the government. At
National Housing Act
the present time those who are building in those villages are, in most cases, people who have come from the city. They have retired and have come from the city in order to live in these villages or they are people who have been unable to build just where they wanted to build in the city and, because they wanted to get away from traffic noise, have moved to the small villages. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few remarks on the housing situation, before the end of the debate. During the discussion, some members who support the government have commented upon the housing program put into effect by the province of Quebec, particularly with regard to the various acts having to do with the housing problem.
I am pleased to remind the house that the province of Quebec benefits at present from the most generous legislation there is in respect to small homes. It is so because the province of Quebec has passed, with respect to housing, an act under which anyone who builds a house may be granted a direct loan from the provincial government in the sense that part of the interest the new owner has to pay on the mortgage is paid back to him; because of this provision, that piece of legislation is one of the most generous there is in the field of housing in the whole of Canada. The province of Quebec has lent many millions of dollars, thus contributing to lighten the new home owner's crushing burden of carrying charges.
It is all very well to say that the federal government is passing legislation in order to make it easier for small owners to obtain the credit required to build houses, but one must not forget that the main obstacle put in the path of prospective builders of houses is the excessive burden of carrying charges. The builder of a house finds that the rent is too high, that this monthly payment cannot be met.
The province of Quebec having undertaken to pay back part of the interest to the prospective owner of a small home, the owner is in a position to borrow a larger amount of money without being crushed by excessive carrying charges.
Various government members from the province of Quebec have claimed that the

National Housing Act government of that province was putting obstacles in the way of various municipalities by failing to take advantage of loan facilities offered by the federal government in the field 'of municipal services, through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, thus preventing those municipalities from opening up new residential districts. Well, I must remind the house that the present rate asked by the Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation on loans to municipalities for the purpose of providing municipal services is much too high. The legislation has been a source of disappointment in the province of Quebec because most municipalities can borrow money from ordinary sources at a much lower rate of interest; that is why, in the province of Quebec, municipal authorities have refused to take advantage of this legislation.
Now, much has been made of the fact that the province of Quebec has not seen fit to take advantage of those sections of the National Housing Act that would have enabled her to do away with slums. Well, Mr. Speaker, as far as that matter is concerned, I hope that the two governments will come to an agreement. As member for the city of Three Rivers, where the most crammed housing conditions are probably to be found, where families are more huddled together than anywhere else, I believe that there is a lot of slum clearing to be done. However, I am rather disappointed when I realize that the present legislation does not bring any improvement in that respect and that it still remains practically impossible for most municipalities in Quebec to take advantage of the sections of the housing act relating to slum clearance. As a matter of fact, it is provided in the act that both the federal and the provincial governments may provide money for slum clearing purposes. Unfortunately, the municipalities are not in a position to accept those gifts from the federal and provincial governments, as their financial situation does not enable them to become real estate agents or to undertake projects of that kind.
Which means, in fact, that the real crux of the matter in so far as the housing problem is concerned is not that our municipalities have trouble getting credit, but that they are quite without the means to face their obligations.
Our municipalities are poor and each time one of them attempts to benefit in some way from the terms of the present act, it is almost immediately faced with bankruptcy and put under the obligation to appeal to the provincial municipal board in order that its debts may be guaranteed by the province.


To my mind it would be a relatively easy matter to solve these problems if each level of government-federal, provincial and municipal-had distinct and well determined sources of revenue. Our municipalities are in a deplorable financial situation and until a conference is held once more to draw a dividing line between the various federal, provincial and municipal fields of taxation, I believe that the housing problem will remain acute in this country.
It is to be regretted that in a country as rich as ours, where there is no lack of building materials and where people will go to any length to become home owners, the present government can find nothing better than to introduce, every two or three years, new legislation which, no doubt, contains a few improvements but which is no solution to the problem as a whole.
In my opinion the government could do better. The problem could be solved, if not once and for all, at least in an equitable fashion, if only the question of sources of tax revenue of the various governments were once more examined and settled on a basis of justice and fairness for all.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure most people in Canada will realize that the government that preceded the present one did a great deal towards solving the housing problem in Canada. We see evidence of that on all sides as we pass through cities, towns and villages throughout the country. Our cities are expanding at a terrific rate, and a good deal of the housing expansion has been aided by the national housing program of the previous administration. On that evidence, I think every fair-minded person will admit that to be so.
The present administration, seeing that a wider field must be covered, has made a very serious attempt to expand this service and provide still more housing. I realize, as I think we all do, that the bill has not yet been finally hammered into shape, and that the discussion that has taken place here has been by way of offering suggestions to those members who will sit on the committee which is going to finish the job. We hope that the outcome of their work will be such that the housing situation we have had during previous years will be improved.
Having said that, I want to point out that I believe there are many areas in Canada which are in a position similar to the one in which I live. I come from an entirely rural

area extending from Regina to the Manitoba boundary in the region south of Qu'Appelle river valley, and it is one of the predominantly agricultural areas of Saskatchewan. As a matter of fact, it is a pioneering area, and we have developed agriculture along all lines. We have a great cattle population, a mixed farming area, and south and west of Regina some of the finest and largest wheat fields to be found anywhere in North America. The riding is predominantly agricultural, and there is not one city in the whole area. It is served by towns, villages and hamlets, and there is a demand and need for housing in all the towns along the main line and spur lines of the C.N.R. In these towns and villages there are people who work in garages, with the implement companies, who operate service stations, teach in the schools and do all those things which service that agricultural area.
I am afraid that in these cities-I am thinking of cities all the time because my constituency extends almost up to the city of Regina-in these towns and villages, the level of earnings of these people is not such that they will fit into this scheme. While the committee is hammering the bill into its final form, perhaps it might give consideration to the lower income people who are providing these services for agriculture in my riding.
As far as the rural people are concerned, there are families with two or three sons. One son may be married, and he can get hold of some land, but he cannot build a house. After he has secured his equipment he probably does not have the down payment on a house. With the amount of the down payment being what it is now, I do not think that the bill, as it stands at the present time, will go very far in helping these people. I offer the suggestion that it would help a great deal if the down payment could be made of such a size as to cover the fees for processing the papers and take care of the insurance which is also being amortized. Perhaps that is too drastic. It will make the down payment low but it would be a great help. Many of these workers who provide these services have a hard time saving $800 or $1,000. By the time the end of the month comes their cheque is gone to the butcher, the baker, the candlestick maker and so on, and they are waiting for their next cheque.
My suggestion is that some very concentrated high-priced thinking, if I may call it that, be put to work on the question of lowering the down payment. I am not saying anything about lengthening the period of amortization. That is the way business is done, and 83276-1001
National Housing Act
I do not think a man who wants to have a home of his own is going to be particularly concerned about that. As long as he is investing his money in that home it will still be all right with him even if it takes him 25 years to pay off his debt. The reason why I suggest lowering the down payment is that repayment is guaranteed in any event. It is all sewed up. Under this situation the lender cannot lose. The money is there, and that is why 1 advocate lowering the down payment. I am just putting forward this view as a suggestion because, as I said when I began my remarks, 1 realize that the bill is not in its final form.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take only a few minutes to praise the government for having introduced this bill, and I wish to congratulate the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) on the way in which he presented this piece of legislation.
Speaking here on November 30, I urged that small cities and rural municipalities be granted the right to benefit from the new legislation. Up to now, as everyone knows, the Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation, as well as lending companies, were reluctant to grant loans outside large centres; so much red tape was involved that the applicants, getting tired of delays and evasive answers, withdrew their claims.
In my opinion, the housing legislation must be accessible to all, wherever they may live, as long as they comply with the basic conditions and provide the necessary guarantees of repayment.
I believe the act will have good results and will attain its object only if all taxpayers can take full and equal advantage of it.
In the second place, newly-wed couples should get help under this new legislation. If a young family man wants to take advantage of the act and if his situation offers the guarantee required under the act, his application should get special attention. Young married couples are just starting in life and have long years of married life ahead of them. By helping them to become home owners not only do we make them savings-minded and provide them with the opportunity to save, but we also make them cling all the more to this land of ours and help them become better citizens.
To make home ownership available to the greatest possible number of people is a social duty, and the government is to be congratulated on the efforts it has made to that end.

National Housing Act
As for myself, I believe this new legislation will promote the development and prosperity of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Public Works):
subsubtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I wish to thank all hon. members, Mr. Speaker, who have taken part in this very interesting debate. That a considerable amount of interest has developed in the subject of housing is well evidenced by the fact that some 53 speakers have participated in this debate. If one can call this a speech in rebuttal, it will make 54 speeches in all. I wish to say a word of thanks especially *to those members on this side of the house who have been so generous in their commendation of this legislation, and in their support of what the government believes is a measure which will go a long way towards helping housing in Canada.
The legislation before the house now is intended to increase the number of houses built each year. We hope to provide assistance to enable Canadians in the low and moderate income brackets to acquire suitable accommodation. I may say that it is intended to improve upon legislation which, since the middle of 1945, has encouraged the construction in Canada of over 730,000 housing units, which is a record unsurpassed in any other country. This Bill No. 102 is designated as an act to promote the construction of new houses, the repair and modernization of existing houses and the improvement of housing and living conditions.
Despite what some hon. members opposite have said about this bill, it is an honest effort to improve upon legislation that now exists, and which has already seen a great record of accomplishment. In 1953 alone, there was a record number of about 105,000 starts.

speechtext: I think the minister will agree that not all were under the act.

subsubtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I readily agree with that, Mr. Speaker, and I have said so. This is an effort by all Canadians who are concerned with the house building business, encouraged, aided and abetted by the government under the terms of the National Housing Act.
I should like to refer to some of the remarks made by some hon. members. Since there were over 50 speakers, I am sure hon. members will understand that I cannot reply to each one of them. I am sure hon. members, too, will agree with the remarks

of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), who said that many of the points were repetitious but were made for the purpose of emphasis. Many of the points that were brought up were raised on more than one occasion. At the outset I would particularly refer to the speech of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), which I thought was a constructive contribution to the debate. As usual, the hon. member had done his homework thoroughly and had analysed the legislation fairly well. He was not able to see it as the forward-looking legislation which the government considers it to be, but I am sure as time goes by he will realize that it is. He took some two hours, well taken, to state the views of the opposition, but some 20 other hon. members from the Progressive Conservative opposition felt that this legislation was so comprehensive it was incumbent upon them to state the views of their party before the debate wound up.
The hon. member referred to the extension of credit, which is the main purpose of this legislation. It was the fear that mortgage money would not continue to flow at the level required for the high rate of house building now attained in this country, which led to these other steps being' taken. I am in complete agreement with his statement that to sustain the financial requirements of a program of 100,000 units in Canada, there must be either an expansion of direct lending or some other means found to attract mortgage funds. This is the very purpose of the bill, as was stated today by the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Enfield), in a splendid contribution to the debate.
I am sure the hon. member agrees with me that it is better to attract mortgage funds from other sources than to expand direct lending by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Regarding the maximum sales price, to which he also referred, I wish to confirm that it is the intention to continue the maximum sales price arrangement. This technique, of course, is not without its troubles. I believe the high level of loans proposed must be accompanied by this limitation. It would be most unfortunate if the increase in the amount of mortgage loans had the effect of an increase in the sales price so that the home owner required as large a down payment and ended up with more mortgage debt.
The hon. member expressed the opinion that part I of the National Housing Act has been as fruitful as any piece of legislation enacted by this parliament or which is likely

to be enacted in the ordinary course of events. The principal purpose of this legislation is to ensure that part I remains effective. We are attempting to cope with the danger that, in its present form, it would become less effective under the developing circumstances. I mentioned this when introducing this legislation.
The hon. member dealt at some length with the implication of steps taken by an approved lender to claim under the insurance policy. He stated that if a mortgagee permits arrears of interest to accumulate beyond six months he is running the risk of losing the benefit of the guarantee with respect to any additional arrears. Perhaps I should clarify this condition. The bill provides that the amount paid in the insurance policy shall include interest at the mortgage rate for six months, and at the mortgage rate less 2 per cent for the ensuing 12 months. The bill also provides that when three months' instalments are in arrears the lender shall report to Central Mortgage the steps being taken. This, I think, is a prudent provision because the insurer is entitled to some indication, not only of his probable losses but also that the lender is being prudent in the administration of the account. Providing such notification is given, then the approved lender qualifies for the interest which runs from six to eighteen months.
If such notification is not given, then the interest included in the payments of the lender is limited to six months at the mortgage rate. This requirement of notification at the end of three months does not imply that foreclosure must be instituted at that time. I would think that in most cases the mortgagee would inform Central Mortgage that they were nursing the account along in the hope that the borrower would cure the default. Under the present joint lending arrangements, there is a similar requirement for notification at the end of three months. In this respect the new bill represents a change only to the extent that interest from six to eighteen months is dependent upon Central Mortgage being notified of the steps being taken by the lender. The hon. member pointed out that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation becomes the sole arbiter in respect of standards and quality of construction. To the extent that present inspections of lending institutions are checked by Central Mortgage, this is presently the case.
I appreciate the reservation of the hon. member. However, over the last few years it has been necessary to superimpose compliance inspections by Central Mortgage upon
National Housing Act
inspections carried on by lending institutions. There is a wide variation in the sufficiency of present inspections, and the new arrangement will have the benefit of uniformity. Furthermore the banks are in no position to do compliance inspections.
The hon. member then went on to deal with the possibility that progress advances will not be handled expeditiously by Central Mortgage. In the case of present lending institutions, they will make their own progress advances, and there will be no change. I do not share the hon. member's view in this respect. In support of this, I point out that houses built under the defence workers' plan in Toronto have been completed more speedily than average joint loans in that area.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), who was the official spokesman,
I presume, of the C.C.F. party, made a speech which followed well the philosophy which is representative of that party. He was concerned with subsidized housing and he said that nowhere in the legislation did he see provision for subsidization. Well, I know that my hon. friend just for the moment overlooked section 35, which has been on the statute books since 1949, and which has been applied in many provinces across this country to enable the people who cannot pay economic rentals to obtain satisfactory accommodation. Perhaps he misunderstood the section in this present bill which continues to provide that three-quarters of such rent reduction fund is borne by the federal government.
Under this legislation there are already 1,562 subsidized rental units in six provinces, the average subsidy unit per month is $17.91, and the share of the federal government on such subsidies is $13.43.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) made reference to housing for elderly persons, a subject which comes up from time to time in this house. I share his favourable view upon the project to which he refers. However, he said all these projects have been made possible by cash subsidies- on the initial cost of construction-from the province, and goes on to say that there is no other subsidy involved in the operation of these units.
I would point out to the hon. member that all of these units were financed under section 9 of the National Housing Act, and I am quite sure that the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) would support me in saying that loans under the National Housing Act and, as well, subsidies from the
1574	HOUSE OF
National Housing Act
government of British Columbia have made these units possible. In that respect I thank the hon. member for Vancouver East for the remarks he made on that subject this afternoon.
I just wish to add, in passing, that I thank the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) for the gracious manner in which he withdrew his reference to an employee of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, made at a time when he was obviously misinformed as to the qualifications and the employment of that employee.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) made a quite substantial contribution to this debate, within the confines- of the socialist philosophy.

speechtext: That makes it a really worthwhile contribution.
