speechtext:
The government, however, believes in making it possible for private enterprise to do as much of the job as possible and then-and only then-for the state to participate. The hon. member suggested that the only possible solution for those in the middle and lower income groups is a low rental housing program, with an element of subsidy in it.
May I remind him, as I did the hon. member for York South, that this legislation exists and that there is subsidized low rental housing in Canada. I am sure that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would be the first to agree that local participation is necessary. The federal government participates, as he well knows, to the extent of 75 per cent of the capital cost, and operating losses, looking to the province and/or the municipality for the remaining 25 per cent.
The hon. member will recall that a project of some 800 units in the city of Winnipeg was placed before the ratepayers last October. I would agree with him that there is need for such a project in Winnipeg; but the ratepayers decided otherwise.
All through this debate there have been inferences that the federal government can do anything in the field of housing. We have listened to some hon. members ask for lower standards of housing. We have listened to other hon. members say that the housing program is entirely too small, and that the federal government should build twice as many houses.
I would remind hon. members again-and I refer to the splendid speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter)-that whereas stimulation and [DOT]assistance for housing can come from the TMr. Winters.]

federal government, in the final analysis it is the municipality which decides the amount of housing to be built.
Then, the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) expressed the views of the Social Credit party. The hon. member brought to my attention a clause in the mortgage deed to create remedies upon default at the end of one month. The member goes on to imply that at the end of that time the owner loses all equity in his home. Let me remind him that the equity of redemption is not automatically lost by virtue of a clause in the contract. Action must be taken in the courts. It is the invariable practice of our judges to do everything in their power to protect the owner's equity of redemption.
The hon. member suggested that we make money available to municipalities and they in turn lend it to home owners. This seems to be a variation of the suggestions of socialist members who wish Central Mortgage to provide money directly to all home owners. I would remind the hon. member for Bow River that immediately after world war I exactly what he proposes was done by the federal government in lending $25 million to municipalities in Canada, with a guarantee by provincial governments. The results, which are a matter of record, were far from happy.
The hon. member for Broadview made what I believe was an extraordinary speech. He is not in the house this evening, and I am sorry for that. I hope that later on he will be here when we have an opportunity of expressing our views on this measure. Twice during the course of his remarks he termed this legislation a gigantic bluff. Then he went on to say, among other things, that there is no indication that there is going to be any more mortgage money available than is available at the present time. I think I should perhaps remind the hon. member that the purpose of authorizing the banks to extend insured loans is to make more mortgage money available. The hon. member suggested that we will all agree that the cheapest house that can be bought today, financed under the National Housing Act, is one costing $10,000. He then went on to indicate the income requirements to carry the mortgage on such a house.
I have just checked with Central Mortgage, who tell me that in 1953 approximately 25 per cent of the houses for home ownership were below $10,000 in cost. He took the example of a $10,000 house, and gave the impression that anybody with an income of less than $3,860 a year need not apply for a loan under the National Housing Act.

Mr. Speaker, some houses during the past year were built for $8,600 under the National Housing Act, which when applying the 23 per cent formula can be acquired by an individual with an income of $2,600 a year.
In dealing with ratio of debt service to income he suggested that the individual be allowed to spend more than 23 per cent of his income on the carrying charges on his home. There is nothing to prevent that happening.
The hon. member for Broadview has apparently been somewhat mixed on this subject. The point at issue is an opinion of mortgage lenders, not only Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The mortgage risk becomes undesirable when there is a mandatory debt service in excess of 23 per cent of the income of the borrower. It is merely a modern manifestation of the old rule that a man cannot normally afford a monthly rent of more than one week's pay. I think it would be doubtful kindness on the part of the government to ask anybody to carry more of a debt burden than he could normally afford.
The hon. member suggested further that Central Mortgage alter its building specifications to allow less costly types of construction.
I would suggest to the hon. member that he have a good look at the building requirements of the city of Toronto, for example, and then come to his own conclusions as to whether much could be accomplished as a result of this suggestion. He also suggests that the amortization period should be lengthened to 30 years. If he will refer again to the bill, as I am sure he has done-and, Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to see him in his seat now-he will see that for home ownership, loans may be made up to 30 years.
The hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis) spoke of the Lowren Housing Company, to which I had occasion to refer earlier today. I pointed out that this project in Ottawa was made possible by loans under the limited dividend section of the act, which provides accommodation for people at reasonable rentals; and to the extent that housing is required in the city of Ottawa for families of lesser incomes within the facilities of section 35-that is section 35 of the old act-the federal-provincial arrangements are available to the province and the municipality, just as they are to the province of Quebec, to reply to the speech made by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) and earlier today by the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne).
The hon. member for Regina City said: "We are the only ones in the country to suggest subsidized housing." He then went on
National Housing Act
to say that the government chose to ignore the representations on the need for subsidized housing. I of course cannot agree with his statement because the federal government introduced section 35, which provides for subsidized housing. I am sure the hon. member does not wish to create the impression that provision for subsidized housing does not exist under the National Housing Act. As a matter of fact, it was we who suggested section 35 to the Saskatchewan government back in 1949. The main impression I gained from the speech made by the hon. member for Regina City was that he carried his philosophy to the point where he believes it is the sole responsibility of the federal government, on behalf of the taxpayers of Canada, to provide not only a home, but a brand new home for every Canadian, whether he wants it or not. That is an objective that I am sure would be viewed with great interest by the taxpayers, and especially the many who have already bought and paid for their homes. I venture to suggest that there are a number of hon. members in this chamber who have never built a house for themselves but are still adequately and comfortably housed, and I, Mr. Speaker, am one of them.
The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) opened his remarks by calling the legislation a delusion, a mockery and a snare. He concluded his remarks by saying that he could not see his way clear to vote against the bill. He referred to the requirement by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for houses of 1,150 and 1,200 square feet. No such requirement exists, Mr. Speaker. Houses are financed by Central Mortgage even below 800 square feet, always provided that room sizes meet standards. The hon. member says that he sees nothing in the world wrong, for example, with houses of 750 to 800 square feet. A man with a wife and four children might have a rather different view.
I now refer to the speech of the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Vincent), who also raised the question about whether or not the province of Quebec is eligible to participate under section 35. This is the section enabling the federal government and the provincial governments to participate under the 75-25 per cent partnership arrangement. I wish to assure him that Quebec will be welcomed into that arrangement at any time the government of Quebec sees fit to take such action.
The hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) referred to the slum clearance provisions of the bill and asked whether they were available in the larger cities. The hon. member cited circumstances in a city which he left

National Housing Act
unnamed, but which I presume to be Saint John, and asked whether the arrangements were available there. I refer to that simply to tell him-and I am sure he would be interested to know it-that conversations are under way with that city toward the clearance of substandard housing in the centre of the city. In fact, one of the undertakings now under discussion is the widening of Main street at the westerly approach to the new viaduct. The hon. member for Royal, I know, would join with me in welcoming the clearance of the unsatisfactory housing conditions in that area.
The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) said that this legislation will result in putting a larger number of people under a larger amount of debt over a longer period of time. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is exactly the end result of this legislation. There is not a single member who spoke in this debate who did not ask for just that. I have always said, and I wish to remind the house, that a low down payment is not an unmixed blessing. It adds to the debt burden, and the longer period of amortization simply increases the period over which the debt must be paid. But it does have the effect of enabling people with lower incomes to get a foothold toward the acquisition of new homes.
The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) said that the legislation was a cruel hoax. I presume he will vote against it, although his party expressed themselves as being for the legislation.
I would refer to the speech made by the honourable and gracious member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken). It was her maiden speech in the house and I wish to congratulate her on her effort. She said that no government should debar anybody from getting a house, and with that of course I agree. This government does not seek to debar anybody. This is enabling legislation designed to help people to acquire houses. And, Mr. Speaker, I do not recall many, if any, instances, in the hon. member's constituency where credit-worthy borrowers have not received loans.
The hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. White) was unique in saying that the legislation was generally satisfactory. Then we come to the speech of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Maedonnell) and sure enough he again said that the government is probably doing the right thing, but doing

it in the wrong way. He said it twice, but most pointedly at page 1419 of Hansard, where he remarked:
Everybody has to approve of that, but of course it is possible to do the right thing in the wrong way . . .
He then expressed his great haunting fear of bureaucracy, his fear that we were by this legislation giving Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation too much power under the terms of the regulations. Well, Mr. Speaker, nobody likes a bureaucracy. But I do not think parliament would take very kindly to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation failing to implement the specific wishes of parliament. It is the government's intention to take for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation only the authorities necessary to give effect to the expressed wishes of parliament. For example, there is no use in specifying a 90 per cent loan with a 10 per cent down payment if the act is administered in such a way that lending institutions can make loans of a lesser amount and a higher down payment. There is no use in aiming at the lowest possible rate of interest if the act is so rigid as to require by legislation the charging of a higher rate than might otherwise be possible by regulation. There is no use in directing Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to see to it that a given standard is maintained for new housing in Canada unless Central Mortgage and Housing is given the powers which enable it to achieve that result. I think Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been doing a splendid job in interpreting the government's wishes in the field of housing but it is not the government's intention to give Central Mortgage powers beyond those required to do their job.
The hon. member for Greenwood expressed some fear about Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation establishing the lending value. I thought I had dealt with that subject when I presented this legislation. The banks have no facilities for appraisal at the present moment. Moreover, it is considered by the government that Central Mortgage must be the agency to establish the lending value so as to ensure the maximum loan being made available. There has been no opposition from the banks and the life companies in this respect. The hon. member also branded this legislation as "state socialism" and said it left so little to be done by private enterprise.
I would like to generalize for a few moments, Mr. Speaker. Several hon. members have said that by insuring loans we would

be protecting the lending institutions and nobody else. But, Mr. Speaker, by insuring loans the government hopes to do two essential things: (1) to ensure a continual flow of mortgage money and (2) to safeguard Canada's banking system by guaranteeing the security, liquidity, and negotiability of insured mortgages. Our banking system in this country is regarded by Canadians and by the world as being sound, and we must take the steps that are necessary to maintain that confidence. This insurance is a guarantee to the banks, and the guarantee to the lending institutions. When hon. members say, as they have said, that this is a guarantee to the banks and to nobody else, I think they are making a mistake. The potential home owner who is seeking a mortgage loan under this act is almost certain to be at the same time a depositor in one of the chartered banks of Canada. It seems to me that when the government is guaranteeing mortgage loans it is guaranteeing that fundamental requirement of confidence in our banks. At the same time there is a guarantee of the deposits of people in all income groups who are able also by virtue of this insurance provision to obtain mortgage loans under this legislation. Our concern as a government is not to insure the banks and protect them against loss as such, but rather to insure the banking system generally and consequently the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are depositors and entrust the bank with their savings.
The socialists fear this measure as "a sellout to capitalist exploitation". That was the theme that ran through the speeches of hon. members in that group. The hon. member for Nanaimo, you will recall, Mr. Speaker, went so far as to brand it as a "cruel hoax". The Progressive Conservatives on the other hand, led by the hon. member for Greenwood, said this was state socialism. The member for Broadview said on January 22, as reported at page 1373 of Hansard:
It seems to me that this is simply another example of this government's drift toward socialism, a government which is so fond of professing its adherence to the principles of free enterprise.
Then later on in the same speech, and as reported at the same page, he got a little bit mixed up and said this:
It is guaranteeing the loans anyway, so it might as well go whole hog and make the mortgages available to the people who want them for the purpose of building houses.
Which is exactly what would be done under what they call state socialism.
With the C.C.F. on the one hand saying it is a sell-out to capital exploitation, and the
National Housing Act
Progressive Conservatives asserting it is state socialism, it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that once again the Liberals have found the middle-of-the-road course, the moderate course, Mr. Speaker. I know this will appeal to the majority of Canadians as being the right one.
During the course of the debate we heard about the housing accomplishments in the United States which have been substantial; in Holland which are very creditable; and in Brazil which I know less about. These hon. members gave one the impression of extolling "in enthusiastic tone, all centuries but this and every country but his own". But the situation in the United States is worth thinking about. Housing there is very different from housing in Canada. In the border states conditions are somewhat similar to ours and the type of housing required is like ours. But when one gets south of the Mason-Dixon line, there are very few basements, far less heating is required; houses are less expensive; they are easier to erect; and different types of building material can be used. Therefore, when we attempt to compare the United States' effort directly with the Canadian effort, these factors must be considered. It was pointed out during the debate that the United States target for next year under President Eisenhower's proposed legislation is to be one million units. Our production in 1953 was about 105,000 starts. Their population is eleven times ours; their gross national product	is over sixteen	times	ours;	so	if
their effort were related directly to ours in terms of population their production would be 1,144,000 houses, and if measured in terms of gross national product would be 1,664,000 houses. In other words our effort in this country compares very favourably with the United States. It compares very favourably with any country in the world.
Now,	Mr. Speaker, I	would	like	for	amoment	to take a look	at the	bill	in	itsentirety	and I want to	make	it clear	to
the hon. member for Broadview, the hon. member for Calgary North, the hon. member for Nanaimo, and the hon. member for Regina City, and all these people who have said very harsh things about the bill, just what it is they are criticizing. I would remind hon. members that this bill contains the provisions that were in the other bill. The important change is in part I, which is the major change designed to improve the legislation.
Hon. members have said there is no change. Section 7 (1) (k) is a new section to facilitate
1578	HOUSE OF
National Housing Act
home extension. Section 14 is a re-enactment of the rental insurance with which hon. members are familiar and which has done so much to provide rental accommodation across this country. Section 16 is the limited dividend section under which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation can and does make 90 per cent loans for a maximum of 50 years at the government borrowing rate of interest. Section 23 is the slum clearance section. Section 24 is the home improvement and home extension loans section. Section 36 is the re-enactment of old section 35, the federal-provincial partnership section. Section 38 is the defence workers section. Section 40 is the direct loans section. In reply to my friends the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland) and the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Fraser), I can now give them the assurance that the direct loans provision will, if parliament wishes, be re-enacted. The direct loans provision has resulted in some 6,750 home ownership loans in over 800 communities in Canada since it was enacted a few years ago.
Then we have part V of the act which was put on the statute books by parliament and which is for the purpose of housing research and community planning. The purpose of that section of the act is to raise the standard of housing in Canada. I point out that part, Mr. Speaker, because during the debate so many hon. members demanded that the government permit Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and house builders generally to build a lower standard of house than parliament has directed it to allow. The hon. member for Broadview terms this a gigantic bluff. The hon. member for Calgary North calls it a delusion, a mockery and a snare. The hon. member for Regina City terms it a bitter disappointment to which he is opposed, containing as it does subsidies sections which he loves so dearly. The hon. member for Nanaimo terms it a cruel hoax. In doing so, they must remember that they were referring to the whole bill and not just any one part of it. When they say they oppose the measure, I would point out that they are opposing those sections of the measure which seem to harmonize so closely with their own often-expressed philosophy. I presume that, when they vote against the measure, they will be prepared to bear the consequences of their vote. When the hon. member for Broadview was speaking and termed as a gigantic bluff legislation which is designed to improve upon legislation which last year achieved in this country a record of about 105,000 starts, one must wonder what language he would have used to refer to the 20,000-house effort in 1933 under a Conservative government.
EMr. Winters.]

Mr. Speaker, I think it is well to remind ourselves again just what this legislation has done and what might be expected from this improved legislation. Stimulated by the various provisions of the legislation, Canadians, under Liberal governments, have built over 730,000 houses since the middle of 1945 and established a new record of about 105,000 starts in 1953. In its present form the bill is designed to produce still better results. It represents the best efforts of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and other government departments, the lending institutions and the banks, who have worked together well, long and hard in order to produce a mutually satisfactory arrangement that will work. I am sure that these people would not take too kindly to statements that they were participating in a gigantic bluff, a snare, a mockery, a delusion or a cruel hoax.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that this bill may fall short of our expectations. I do not think so; at the same time it may exceed our expectations. I hope so. We do not guarantee infallibility in its administration. However, I can assure the house that this is an honest effort to make it easier for Canadians of moderate incomes to build homes. It is a sincere attempt to further the government's efforts -and I refer again to the title of the bill- to promote the construction of new houses, the repair and modernization of existing houses, and the improvement of housing and living conditions.
Mr. Speaker, I heard no clear expression of attitude toward this legislation from the members of the Progressive Conservative opposition. The hon. member for Broadview termed the entire legislation-including the slum clearance section, the limited dividend provision, the federal-provincial agreement provisions and all others-a gigantic bluff. The hon. member for Calgary North termed it a snare, a mockery and a delusion. The hon. member for Regina City called it a bitter disappointment. In view of the fact that they have used those terms and because other hon. members have said similar things about this legislation-legislation which I consider to be more comprehensive and all embracing than any similar act enacted by any other sovereign parliament in the world, I think we should know just where hon. members stand. I would therefore ask you, Mr. Speaker, if you would be kind enough, when putting the vote, to call for the yeas and the nays.

I think it is the unanimous opinion of the house, Mr. Speaker, that tomorrow we should discuss external affairs.
For that purpose, we have devised a procedure which will be of this nature. After the orders of the day have been called sufficiently that hon. members have put all their questions which precede that order, the motion will be made that the house do now adjourn. By consent that motion will be debatable, and will be withdrawn when the debate is concluded so that there will be no vote on it. It will supersede the five o'clock interruption, in case the debate continues past that hour. If it is not concluded by ten o'clock, the house will adjourn as usual and the debate will automatically end at that time.
If, however, the debate ends before ten o'clock we shall proceed with the consideration of the Criminal Code in the committee of the whole.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
